Cloud security is less concentrated: the four largest vendors are roughly 35-40% of Gartner's $10.6bn CSPM-plus-CWPP spend for 2025, giving an HHI of about 500-700 [estimate: vendor ARR rolled to end-2025 from each one's last disclosure; the vendor definitions include CIEM, ASPM and DSPM spend that Gartner may classify elsewhere]. The identity pool outside Microsoft (Okta, CyberArk, CrowdStrike) is about $4.9bn, of which CrowdStrike is about 12% [estimate: revenue and ARR mixed across the three].

The gap is closing fastest in identity and SIEM against the incumbents and widening in cloud against Wiz.▪ Wiz added roughly $330m of ARR a year over the eighteen months to March 2026 against CrowdStrike's roughly $200m [estimate: ($1,000m − $500m) over 1.5 years, from two dated secondary figures].

4.5 Market sizing, tested against management's slides

CrowdStrike's published total addressable market has been marked up at every briefing: $25bn at the IPO (2019), $36bn (CY2021), $58bn (CY2022), $76bn (CY2023), $100bn (CY2024), $116bn (CY2025), $140bn (CY2026) and $149bn (CY2026, restated in the Q4 FY2026 deck).▪ The forward figure moved from $106bn (FY2025) to $325bn (CY2030). The near-year figures cite fifteen IDC, Gartner, Forrester and IANS reports; the far-year figures are described on the slide itself as a company estimate that "includes organic category growth, product roadmap, future initiatives and estimated cloud security opportunity" [deck: Fal.Con 2025 2025-09-17, slide 110].

The CY2030 figure of $325bn equals 87% of Gartner's forecast for all information-security spending in 2030 ($372.6bn, a total that includes managed and consulting services and network equipment) and implies a 21.5% compound market rate from CY2026 against Gartner's 10.7% [web, secondary relay]. And CrowdStrike's own share of its own near-year TAM has barely moved: $1.73bn of ARR against a $58bn CY2022 figure is 3.0%; $5.84bn against $149bn is 3.9%▪ [estimate: ending ARR at the deck date over the TAM in the same deck]. The market has been marked up almost as fast as the company has grown.

On the endpoint slice specifically, building bottom-up from CrowdStrike's own revenue and its 17.7% share gives a category of $6.3-8.3bn for the mid-2022 window, $9-13bn for CY2024 and $12-19bn for CY2026 [estimate: §4.6]. The $22bn "Endpoint Security" figure on the current slide is consistent with that only if the category grew near 20% a year throughout. The $26bn "Managed Services" and $23bn "Security & IT Ops" slices are broader categories in which CrowdStrike competes with services firms and IT-management vendors.

At July 31, 2025 management estimated logo penetration below 40% of the Global 2000, about 7% of firms with 251-7,499 employees, below 1% of the more than 50m businesses with 5-250 employees, and below 2% of the public sector▪ [deck: Fal.Con 2025 2025-09-17, slide 102, on company data with D&B Hoovers and Government Navigator]. The same four-panel slide has run since April 2022, and it shows mid-market penetration moving about one point a year and the small-business panel unmoved in four years, despite Falcon Go being built for that segment.

4.6 Share counter-evidence

The largest is Microsoft's gain: from 16.4% to 28.6% of IDC's modern-endpoint category between mid-2022 and CY2024 while CrowdStrike's disclosed share stopped at 17.7%. The mechanism is E5 and now E7 bundling into a base of nearly 1.5m security customers. Against it, CrowdStrike's core residual ARR still grew about 14% in FY2026 and about 18% in the twelve months to July 2026, Gap and Oracle chose Falcon after testing Defender, and IDC's E5 allocation is not verifiable.

Second is Palo Alto's platform consolidation: next-generation security ARR of $9.10bn at July 2026 (+63% including CyberArk, against a $7.0-7.1bn standalone guide, so roughly $2bn of the figure is acquired [estimate: reported base less the standalone guide midpoint]), XSIAM above $700m of ARR with about 1,000 customers, exposure management added to XSIAM, and Koi and Chronosphere bought in FY2026. Palo Alto sells the endpoint inside a SOC bundle, the opposite motion to CrowdStrike's from the endpoint outward.

Third is frontier-lab entry, which analysts pressed on directly at Q4 FY2026. Microsoft announced MAI-Cyber-1-Flash with "better performance than much larger Mythos model but at half the cost" [web]. CrowdStrike's answer is data and in-line enforcement plus partnership: it describes itself as the only cybersecurity company in both Anthropic's Project Glasswing and OpenAI's Trusted Access for Cyber from the start (Q1 FY2027 call), a management claim, and Glasswing's published partner list also includes Palo Alto, Microsoft, Google and Cisco.

Fourth is Microsoft's kernel policy, in Section 2. Fifth is MDR consolidation by vendors that do not own an agent, which has so far moved endpoints onto Falcon. On in-sourcing there is one data point in the other direction: Oracle's chief security officer said the company "attempted to build our own" SIEM and it "didn't work very well" (Fal.Con 2025).

Arithmetic behind the estimates. Mid-2022 endpoint market: CrowdStrike revenue for the twelve months to July 2022 was $1,834m, subscription at 94% is $1,724m, an endpoint-counted portion of 65-85% is $1,120-1,465m, divided by 17.7% gives $6.3-8.3bn. Grown at 15-20% a year: $9-13bn for CY2024, widened to $10-14bn in the share arithmetic below to allow for the top of the base range, and $12-19bn for CY2026. Microsoft CY2024 endpoint revenue: 28.6% of $10-14bn is $2.9-4.0bn. CrowdStrike endpoint modules at January 2025: 55-70% of the $2,942m core residual is $1,620-2,060m, a 12-20% share. HHI mid-2022: 17.7² + 16.4² + 4.6² + 2.8² = 611, where the 16.4% is Microsoft's share inside the disclosed 46.7% legacy block, plus the remaining 30.3% of that block split six ways (153) or as 12/8/5/3/2.3 (247), total about 760-860. CY2024: 28.6² = 818, plus CrowdStrike at 12-20% (144-400), SentinelOne at 6% (36) and the remaining 45-53% across legacy vendors at 5-10% each (300-400), total about 1,300-1,650.

5. Value chain and profit pools

The chain from infrastructure to end customer has six external layers. Amazon Web Services hosts the platform, is the largest single route to market, is a Falcon Complete customer, and competes through GuardDuty and Security Hub. Microsoft supplies the Windows kernel interfaces, sells the substitute inside E5, and from FY2027 also resells Falcon against Azure consumption commitments.▪ Colocation landlords in the US and Germany and a limited number of equipment suppliers provide the owned capacity. Resellers, distributors, global system integrators and MSSPs move the vast majority of sales. And more than 88,000 organizations pay the bill.

One dollar of end-customer spend on a Falcon subscription bought through a reseller, on FY2026 economics:

Layer Named participants Capture per $1.00 Layer gross margin Who sets the price at this interface
Reseller or distributor Optiv, CDW, SHI, GuidePoint, distributors outside the US $0.08-0.18 [estimate: TD SYNNEX 7.0% company gross margin as the floor for the logistics layer, CDW 21.7% as the ceiling for a value-added reseller, and 10-20% partner discounts on published channel guides] [web] CDW 21.7% (2025); TD SYNNEX 7.0% (FY2025) [web] CrowdStrike sets list and partner discount tiers; the reseller sets the end price inside that band
Cloud marketplace, where used AWS, Google, Microsoft $0.015-0.035 of contract value, deducted from CrowdStrike's disbursement fee, not margin AWS publishes the schedule: 3% under $1m, 2% to $10m, 1.5% above, plus 0.5% on channel-partner private offers (docs.aws.amazon.com, accessed 2026-09-02) [web]
CrowdStrike $0.82-0.92 received, of which about $0.63-0.66 is gross profit Subscription 78% GAAP, about 81% non-GAAP CrowdStrike, subject to volume discounts
Hosting: AWS, colocation, equipment AWS; colocation landlords; server suppliers $0.10-0.12 of CrowdStrike subscription revenue [estimate: §5.1] AWS segment operating margin 35.4% in 2025 ($45.6bn on $128.7bn, AMZN 10-K) AWS sets price; CrowdStrike arbitrages between AWS regions and its own capacity
Support, cloud operations, software, amortisation CrowdStrike staff, third-party licences, acquired intangibles $0.10-0.12 of subscription revenue [estimate: the remainder of non-GAAP subscription cost of revenue] labour market labour market
Operating-system vendor Microsoft $0.00 — Microsoft sets kernel-access policy

The channel keeps roughly a dime to twenty cents, CrowdStrike keeps roughly eighty cents of which about two-thirds is gross profit, and the hosting layer receives about a dime. Microsoft takes nothing from this dollar and sells its own bundle against it.▪

5.1 Upstream: the supplier interface changed shape

Subscription gross margin went from 36% (FY2017) to 78% (FY2024-FY2026) while AWS list prices did not move in CrowdStrike's favour in any disclosed way. The margin came from dual-sourcing between AWS and owned colocation, smart filtering, and modules after the first being close to pure gross margin.▪ The CFO described the method as early as December 2019: "we optimize between AWS and our own data centers and we optimize within each data center themselves". Gross data-centre and computer equipment went from $756m (January 2025) to $1,059m (January 2026) to $1,199m (July 2026); property, equipment and lease assets were $855m in the US, $107m in Germany and $84m elsewhere at January 31, 2026.

Hosting-related cost is disclosed once, as a share: "greater than 50%" of non-GAAP cost of revenue at Q2 FY2024 [deck: Fal.Con 2023 2023-09-20, slide 73]. Applied to a reconstructed FY2026 non-GAAP cost of revenue of about $1.06bn, hosting-related cost was roughly $0.5bn, about 10-11% of revenue [estimate: the ">50%" share applied to GAAP cost of revenue of $1,219m less $130m of stock compensation and about $28m of acquired-intangible amortisation; the share has not been updated since 2023 and depreciation of owned equipment has risen since].

The schedule of purchase commitments is the part that changed. Non-cancelable purchase commitments beyond one year:

Date Commitments beyond one year ($m) Ending ARR ($m) Ratio
Jan 31, 2022 178 1,731 10%
Jan 31, 2024 748 3,435 22%
Jan 31, 2025 2,692 4,242 64%
Jan 31, 2026 2,770 5,253 53%
Jul 31, 2026 4,142 5,841 71%
Jul 31, 2026 plus the post-quarter signing ~7,040 5,841 ~120%

The Q2 FY2027 10-Q adds: "Subsequent to July 31, 2026, the Company has committed to an additional $2.9 billion of non-cancelable purchase obligations from fiscal 2027 to fiscal 2034." The commitment schedule at July 31, 2026 is $186m for the rest of FY2027, $843m in FY2028, $844m in FY2029, $652m in FY2030, $378m in FY2031 and $1,239m thereafter. The note describes the commitments as "data center capacity, advertising, technology, equipment, office renovations, corporate events, and consulting services", with data-centre capacity named first and no split given, and no counterparty named.

CrowdStrike is buying capacity ahead of revenue: equipment purchased but not in service went from $162m (January 2026) to $274m (July 2026). And the FY2028 and FY2029 tranches are each 1.6-1.9x FY2026 hosting-related cost of revenue. Absorbing the FY2028 tranche at hosting alone, at the current 10-12% intensity, would need subscription revenue of $7.0-8.4bn against a total FY2027 revenue guide of $6.0bn [estimate: $843m divided by 0.12 and by 0.10]. Because the note bundles advertising, technology, equipment and consulting into the same figure, part of that tranche may not be data-centre capacity.

The owned-colocation model has not produced a gross-margin gap against the AWS-only peers. CrowdStrike's subscription gross margin of 78% GAAP compares with Okta at 80% and Elastic at 81%, both on AWS, and with Zscaler at 77% on its own colocation; the gap it has produced is against SentinelOne at 74%, whose cost base is AWS usage charges at a fifth of CrowdStrike's scale. Scale, module attach and smart filtering explain more of the 78-81% than colocation does.▪ Palo Alto's cloud commitments of $6.58bn at July 2025 against $9.2bn of revenue show that the commitment structure is not unique; SentinelOne ($732m), Zscaler ($608m), Okta ($469m) and Elastic ($614m) commit far less.

5.2 Downstream: channel, marketplaces, and what they cost

Channel share of revenue was disclosed once, at 83% of total revenue in FY2023 (Q4 FY2023 call). The named routes and their scale:

Route Latest figure
AWS Marketplace Nearly $1.5bn of total contract value in FY2026, growing nearly 50%
All cloud marketplaces More than $600m of deal value in Q2 FY2027 alone, +30%
Microsoft Marketplace Open from FY2027; Azure consumption commitments usable on Falcon; two seven-figure Flex wins in Q2 FY2027
MSSP Under $100m to more than $1.3bn in about three years; about 15% of new business in FY2025
Global system integrators Neared $1bn in FY2025 growing above 40%; growing nearly 50% in Q2 FY2027, "largely focused on next-gen SIEM transformations"
Partners above $1bn of cumulative business AWS, Optiv, CDW, SHI, GuidePoint

What the go-to-market motion costs: capitalized contract acquisition costs were $704.6m in FY2026, 14.6% of revenue, comprising sales commissions, associated payroll taxes and referral fees paid to partners without a split between them, with $449.4m amortised into sales and marketing that year. Partner rebates are guided at about 0.8% of FY2027 revenue as contra revenue. Marketplace listing fees were an estimated $22-53m on $1.5bn of AWS contract value [estimate: 1.5-3.5% of TCV on the published AWS schedule]. The reseller discount is outside revenue entirely.

Concentration is the lowest in the peer set. No channel partner or direct customer was 10% or more of revenue or receivables in FY2024-FY2026.▪ SentinelOne's largest partner was 18% of FY2026 revenue; three distributors were 44.2% of Palo Alto's FY2025 revenue; six distributors held 67% of Fortinet's net receivables. The one disclosed instance of channel power moving the other way is the Q3 FY2025 exclusion of "approximately $26 million from ARR after a distributor in the federal space provided notice of its intention to exercise transferability rights", where the revenue stayed in GAAP results and the DOJ and SEC information requests on ARR reporting followed.

Marketplaces do three things. They halve the sales cycle ("it cuts the sales cycle down, when we use the AWS Marketplace, by almost 50%", Q4 FY2020 call). They align the hyperscaler's sales force ("we have actual quota requirement for the sales reps when they sell our stuff in the marketplace", Citi conference, 2020-09-09). And they let the customer pay from a budget already committed to the hyperscaler. In December 2025 AWS made Falcon Next-Gen SIEM the default SIEM in its Security Hub console, with the stated intent "to convert Next-Gen SIEM usage into Flex subscriptions" (Q3 FY2026 call).

5.3 Customer-side economics

A mid-market buyer with managed detection and add-on modules typically pays $200-400 per endpoint per year (costbench.com, checked 2026-08-26, accessed 2026-09-02) [web], a pricing site's estimate against published list prices of $60-185. Management's own return figures are vendor-computed business-value assessments: an average first-year return of 150% across nearly 3,000 customers (2022), 170% across 4,700 assessments (Fal.Con 2022) and "over 200% ROI" for enterprise customers (Q1 FY2024 call), with payback "sometimes... 3- to 6-month".

The outside benchmark is the cost of the event the product prevents. IBM's 2025 study puts the average US data breach at $10.22m and the global average at $4.44m (cyberscoop.com, accessed 2026-09-02) [web]. A 10,000-endpoint US enterprise paying about $3m a year covers its subscription with one avoided average breach every 3.4 years, before any consolidation saving [estimate: $10.22m over $3.0m, using the midpoint of the $200-400 per-endpoint range]. Consolidation is the second source of saving: a state customer saved $6.4m over three years replacing Defender (April 2023 briefing) and the enterprise in the Q1 FY2024 example found E5 $2.3m more expensive, both management-selected cases.

Security is an operating expense for the buyer, so depreciation schedules do not apply. Gartner forecasts worldwide information-security spending of about $240-244bn in 2026, up 11.6-12.5% [web, secondary relay], against which CrowdStrike's FY2027 revenue guide of $5,991-6,011m is about 2.5%. The constraints are substitution and Flex utilisation.

5.4 The binding constraint

Customer procurement was the binding constraint through FY2025 and has loosened. Enterprise sales cycles lengthened about 15% year over year after the incident (Q3 FY2025 call), the marketplace route halves the cycle, and Flex removes per-module procurement. Net new ARR then reached a record $332.8m in Q2 FY2027, up 51%. No physical input constrains output: equipment is bought on purchase orders with no long-term supply contracts, and FY2027 capex is guided at 7-8% of revenue.

The constraint now is contractual. About $7.0bn of non-cancelable commitments against $5.0bn of cash and $1.2bn of FY2026 free cash flow is a fixed cost base being laid down ahead of the growth that fills it, with the composition undisclosed. The exposure is the gross margin: hosting and data-centre depreciation supplied 42-44% of the increase in subscription cost of revenue in FY2026 and Q2 FY2027, and the FY2029 subscription gross-margin target of 82-85% assumes the capacity is used.▪

5.5 Circular flows and vendor financing

Customer purchases of Falcon through the AWS, Google and Microsoft marketplaces are drawn against commitments the customer has already made to the hyperscaler, so part of CrowdStrike's bookings is funded by a prior commitment to a supplier and competitor: more than $600m of deal value went through those rails in Q2 FY2027 alone.

CrowdStrike Financial Services, launched in Q3 FY2025, is vendor financing on the balance sheet. It had provided $230m of cumulative loan value by Q2 FY2026, more than half of it on Flex deals, with 95% funding new logos or platform expansion [deck: Fal.Con 2025 2025-09-17, slide 84]. Financing receivables at amortised cost went from $45.4m (January 2025) to $264.2m (January 2026) to $330.4m (July 2026), with unfunded commitments of $69.7m, and two end users were 27% of financing receivables at January 2026. Management calls the portfolio investment grade; the 10-Q's internal rating table places $168.6m of $330.4m in the 5-6 bucket on a scale where 1 is best, and the mapping from internal ratings to external grades is not stated. Management states the purpose: "we can supersize the Falcon Flex deals and then we can actually finance it" (Morgan Stanley, 2025-03-06). At $330m against $1,236m of FY2026 free cash flow, the cash tied up is about 27% of one year's free cash flow.

The Falcon Funds, two venture vehicles with $60m committed by CrowdStrike and matched by Accel-related entities, held a 9.4% stake in Seraphic before CrowdStrike bought the company thirteen months later, producing a $31.0m remeasurement gain of which $15.5m went to the outside investors.

6. Secular and industry trends

6.1 Growth attribution: where the growth came from

The framing management and the sell-side use is that the three emerging lines are where the growth comes from and the endpoint business is mature. At Fal.Con 2024 an analyst put the arithmetic to management, unchallenged: "based on the $10 billion ARR guide, you're effectively expecting in the aggregate, these 3 high-growth areas to make up about 50% of your total ARR by that point, that's up from roughly 25% today." On the Q2 FY2027 call an analyst described the original franchise as "perceived as a more mature market".

The trailing twelve-month record disagrees about where growth is coming from now:

Twelve months to Total net new ARR ($m) Trio ($m) Core ($m) Core share Core ARR growth
Jul 2025 776 465 311 40% +11.2%
Jul 2026 1,185 620 564 48% +18.3%

Core net new ARR grew 81% year over year while trio net new ARR grew 33%. The core supplied 48% of the last twelve months' additions against 40% the year before, and its own growth rate went from 11.2% to 18.3%.▪ The trio's growth declined from 42% to 39.6% over the same span: cloud from +35% to +29% and SIEM from +95% to +60%, against identity accelerating from +21% (the first quarter on the Shield-inclusive basis) to +34%. The trio still grows roughly 2x as fast as the core in percentage terms; the acceleration in the company's growth rate came from the core. The mix shift management describes did happen through FY2026, with the trio going from 25% of ARR at January 2024 to 36% at January 2026, and then advanced one point in the six months to July 2026.

Management's own commentary matches the arithmetic where its framing does not: "our endpoint business accelerated for the fourth consecutive quarter" (Q2 FY2027 call), and on the runway, "about half the market is still using legacy AV".

Four contributors to the core acceleration are disclosed and none is separately sized: legacy-antivirus displacement; AI workloads as new protected units ("Nonhuman identities and agents require their own underlying host, creating greenfield demand for sensors", Q1 FY2027 call); AIDR, whose ARR grew more than 250% sequentially in Q1 FY2027 and nearly tripled again in Q2 from an undisclosed base; and Exposure Management with Falcon for IT, whose adoption "nearly double[d] year-over-year" in Q1 FY2027. Acquired ARR is a small part: SGNL and Seraphic contributed $7.8m of net new ARR in Q1 FY2027, about 3% of that quarter's total, and the XM Cyber assets bring no ARR and are excluded from guidance.

6.2 Growth against the market and against the peer cohort

Building a denominator from the seven listed security vendors with full data (CrowdStrike, Palo Alto, SentinelOne, Zscaler, Fortinet, Okta, Check Point), each on its own fiscal year:

Fiscal year Cohort revenue ($m) Cohort YoY CrowdStrike revenue ($m) CrowdStrike share
FY2020 9,613 — 481 5.0%
FY2021 12,241 +27% 874 7.1%
FY2022 16,296 +33% 1,452 8.9%
FY2023 20,751 +27% 2,241 10.8%
FY2024 24,656 +19% 3,056 12.4%
FY2025 28,805 +17% 3,954 13.7%

Fiscal year-ends differ across the cohort, so each row mixes as-of dates by up to six months. CrowdStrike's revenue compounded at 52.3% a year over FY2020-FY2025; the cohort compounded at 24.6%; CrowdStrike's share of the cohort compounded at 22.3% (5.0% to 13.7%), and 1.246 multiplied by 1.223 reproduces the 52% company rate. Gartner's information-security spending grew about 12-13% a year over the same span [web, secondary relay]. So the 52% splits into roughly 12-13 points of market growth, about 11 points of the listed next-generation cohort taking spend from legacy vendors, in-house budgets and services, and about 22 points of CrowdStrike taking share inside that cohort. Share gain inside the cohort was the largest single contributor.▪

In the latest comparable quarter that rate has halved. Cohort revenue including CrowdStrike grew 25.9% and CrowdStrike's share went from 16.67% to 16.64%; removing the $388m of Chronosphere and CyberArk revenue that Palo Alto's 10-Q discloses, the cohort grew 20.0% and CrowdStrike's share rose 0.79 of a point. Over FY2020-FY2025 the average annual gain was 1.74 points. The reason is that the cohort accelerated alongside CrowdStrike.▪

That matters for how the FY2027 acceleration is attributed. Year-over-year revenue growth by quarter, from the April-June 2025 quarter to the latest available: CrowdStrike +6.0 points, Fortinet +12.0, Cloudflare +8.1, Zscaler +2.8, SentinelOne −2.3, Okta −0.9, Palo Alto −1.1 organic. Four vendors accelerated and three decelerated. The four that accelerated all sell into infrastructure that AI consumption expands; two of the three that decelerated sell a single mature control point, endpoint-only at SentinelOne and workforce identity at Okta. SentinelOne is the sharper test because it bought two AI-security assets in the same window and its ARR still decelerated to +22%. Management attributes its own acceleration to a company-specific event, the April 2026 frontier-model releases and the coalition it convened afterwards. The growth effect is not company-specific: Fortinet accelerated twice as much and Cloudflare a third more over the same calendar window without either programme. CrowdStrike's acceleration is mid-cohort in magnitude and upper-quartile in level.

Against Microsoft, the comparison cannot be closed. Microsoft reported 28.6% IDC share for CY2024 with revenue growing 28.2%, which implies the IDC-defined market grew about 16% that year [estimate: 1.282 x 25.8 / 28.6 − 1]. CrowdStrike's core ARR grew about 14% over the year to January 2025, so in the incident year the endpoint franchise grew at or below the category while Microsoft gained 2.8 points. The direction reversed from CY2025 on CrowdStrike's own figures.

6.3 Durable against cyclical

Net new ARR has moved through a full budget-and-event cycle:

Fiscal year Net new ARR growth Driver, per management
FY2022 +51% remote-work demand
FY2023 +22% "increased macroeconomic headwinds"; non-enterprise days-to-close +11%
FY2024 +6% a 10% first-half headwind to net new ARR
FY2025 (8)% the July 19 incident; Q3 net new ARR $153m; sales cycles about 15% longer
FY2026 +25% Flex, the expiry of commitment packages, endpoint re-acceleration
FY2027 guide +34% AI-security demand from April 2026; record Q3 pipeline

Peak to peak from FY2022 to the FY2027 guide, net new ARR compounded at about 15% a year; trough to trough from FY2021 to FY2025, about 16%. A through-cycle net new ARR growth rate near 15% puts FY2027's 34% at a cyclical high and FY2025's decline down to a company-specific event. Two-year stacks separate easy laps from real acceleration: Q4 FY2026's $330.7m against Q4 FY2024's $282m is an 8% two-year rate, Q1 FY2027's $255.8m against $212m is 10%, and Q2 FY2027's $332.8m against $217.6m is 24%. The Q2 acceleration survives the test. The Q3 FY2027 guide of $343-347m is measured against a Q3 FY2026 base that had itself grown 73% off the incident trough of $153m, so its headline +29-31% overstates; against Q3 FY2024's $223.1m it is a 16% three-year rate.

One arithmetic constraint on the forward path: subscription revenue grew 27.0% in Q2 FY2027 while ending ARR grew 25.4%. ARR is the forward run-rate that revenue converges toward, so revenue cannot compound faster than ARR indefinitely, and today's 25-26% revenue growth is catching up to an ARR base compounding at 25%.▪ Bloomberg consensus revenue growth of 22% for FY2028 is consistent with that convergence.

6.4 The budget backdrop, and the disagreement inside it

The two external budget series disagree, and CrowdStrike's own TAM chart cites both. Gartner has 2026 information-security spending at $248.9bn growing 12.7% in constant currency and 10.7% a year to $372.6bn in 2030 [web, secondary relay]. The IANS Research and Artico Search survey of 587 CISOs, fielded April to August 2025, recorded security budgets growing 4% in 2025, the lowest in five years and down from 8% in 2024, with security falling to 10.9% of IT spend from 11.9% [web]. The populations differ: Gartner counts end-user spending including services and network hardware, IANS counts CISO-controlled budgets.

CrowdStrike's explanation for growing 25-34% against a 4-13% backdrop has two parts, one evidenced and one not. Consolidation is evidenced: Flex-adopted ending ARR reached $2.29bn at July 2026, +101%, 39% of total ARR, with the uplift ladder in Section 1.3 and more than 630 accounts re-Flexed at least once, 6x the year-earlier count. Incremental AI budget is management's own account: "2 years ago, there wasn't these big token budgets... people are finding money, and it's incremental" (Q1 FY2027 Q&A). The IANS 2026 benchmark, the first independent test of that claim, had not been published as of 2026-09-02.

6.5 Where the slope is steepest

Region Q2 FY2027 revenue ($m) Q2 FY2026 ($m) Growth Share
United States 954.5 784.7 +21.6% 65% (from 67%)
EMEA 263.7 188.4 +40.0% 18% (from 16%)
Asia Pacific 157.9 117.5 +34.3% 11% (from 10%)
Other 94.8 78.3 +21.1% 6% (from 7%)
International total 516.4 384.3 +34.4% 35%

International revenue grew 13 points faster than US revenue and reached 35% of the total. The forward growth rate depends increasingly on geographies where the installed base is thinner, which supports its durability and raises exposure to European procurement cycles, data-sovereignty rules and currency. The sovereignty build-out is visible in the asset base ($107m of German property and equipment against $855m in the US) and in the Schwarz Digits STACKIT partnership announced in March 2026.

6.6 What changes the slope

Up: AI agents as a new protected unit, which converts AI adoption into unit growth on the existing pricing model, with CrowdStrike's own telemetry showing more than 400% growth in Claude usage and more than 100% growth in custom agent usage on protected endpoints in recent months. Legacy SIEM replacement, where Cisco's security revenue including Splunk grew 2% in FY2026 and Elastic's subscription revenue 15% against CrowdStrike's SIEM at 60%. Identity consolidation into platforms. Cyber-insurance underwriting as the compelling event in the small-business segment, with Coalition, Liberty Mutual, Lockton, Resilience and Marsh joining Project QuiltWorks in Q1 FY2027 to underwrite frontier AI model risk. And marketplace routes that neutralise part of the bundling advantage: Azure consumption commitments became spendable on Falcon in FY2027.

Down: Microsoft's endpoint bundle and its kernel policy, both in Section 2. Cloud-security consolidation, where Google closed Wiz in March 2026 and CrowdStrike's cloud growth declined from +80% to +29% over two years while the hyperscaler consumption it protects grew 37-41%. What ARR measures under Flex, where utilisation was last given as above 75% at Q2 FY2026 and the 10-K warns of contraction if commitments are not consumed. And contract duration flattering the backlog: remaining performance obligations went from $7.2bn (July 2025) to $10.7bn (July 2026), +49%, while ARR grew 25% and the portion due within twelve months went from 52% to 46%, so most of the RPO growth is Flex lengthening contracts.

6.7 Management's market sizing against its own capture assumption

Between Fal.Con 2024 and Fal.Con 2025 the company restated its product-line markets and, on the same two slides, its illustrative FY2031 scale for each line:

Line TAM, previous view (CY2028) TAM, current view (CY2030) FY2031 scale, previous FY2031 scale, current Implied capture, previous Implied capture, current
Cloud Security $31bn $49bn $2.5-3.0bn $2.5-3.0bn 8.9% 5.6%
Next-Gen Identity $17bn $19bn $1.0-1.5bn $1.0-1.5bn 7.4% 6.6%
Next-Gen SIEM $16bn $48bn $1.0-1.5bn $1.5-2.0bn 7.8% 3.6%

The cloud market rose 58% with no change to the illustrative scale, and the SIEM market tripled with a $0.5bn increase in scale. On management's own two slides the assumed share of its own addressed markets by FY2031 falls by a third in cloud and by more than half in SIEM.▪

The long-range ARR targets embed a deceleration of their own. From the FY2027 guide midpoint of $6.61bn, $10bn by January 2031 needs a 10.9% compound rate and average net new ARR of about $850m a year over FY2028-FY2031, which is 37% below the FY2027 guide.▪ Holding FY2027's guided net new ARR flat and never growing it again delivers $10bn during FY2030. The trio's illustrative FY2031 scale sums to $5.0-6.5bn, leaving a residual core of $3.5-5.0bn against $3.66bn at July 2026, a core compound rate between −1% and +7% over four and a half years against a realized +18.3%. Either the $10bn target is set well below the run-rate, or the trio illustration overstates the future mix; the consensus path and the realized core record both support the first.

6.8 What would move first if the thesis were breaking

Ordered by how early each moves:

  • Professional services revenue, already at +7% in Q2 FY2027, with the cause unresolved. Incident-response and readiness engagements precede subscription lands by one to three quarters.
  • New-logo net new ARR and the Flex new-logo share, a record and 34% of net new ARR in Q2 FY2027. New logos are the first casualty of a budget freeze, as in Q3 FY2023.
  • The re-Flex count and interval, 630 accounts with a first re-Flex at eight months on average. A lengthening interval means committed value is being consumed more slowly, a year before it touches revenue.
  • Core ARR growth falling back below the trio's, which would mean the endpoint re-acceleration was a two-year AI-adoption pulse.
  • Cloud ARR growth below 25%, at which point the FY2031 illustrative scale stops being reachable without a step-change.
  • Net retention below 112% or gross retention below 97%, which would mean consolidation had stopped adding wallet share.
  • Current remaining performance obligations converging on ARR growth, about 32% against 25% now, which would mean the Flex duration extension had run its course.

7. Critical points

1. The growth is coming from the endpoint business, which analysts describe as mature. Core ARR outside cloud, identity and SIEM grew 11.2% in the twelve months to July 2025 and 18.3% in the twelve months to July 2026, and supplied 48% of the last twelve months' net new ARR against 40% the year before. Over the same span the emerging trio decelerated from 42% to 39.6%, with cloud and SIEM both slowing. The trio still grows about twice as fast in percentage terms, and it is no longer the source of the change in the company's growth rate.

2. Cloud Security has added about $200m of ARR a year for four consecutive twelve-month windows while its growth rate declined from above 80% to above 29%, and its FY2031 illustrative range of $2.5-3.0bn needs a 25-30% compound rate from $905m over four and a half years, which is today's rate with no further deceleration allowed. At the current dollar add the line reaches about $1.8bn by January 2031, $0.7bn below the bottom of that range.▪ Meanwhile Wiz passed $1bn of ARR before Google closed its $32bn purchase in March 2026, reaching roughly 40% of the Fortune 100 [web], and it is now sold by a hyperscaler. This is the one line where a larger competitor is growing at least as fast.

3. Free cash flow after stock compensation has not grown in five years. Free cash flow less stock compensation was $143m in FY2021 and about $140m in FY2026; per share it declined from about $0.16 to about $0.14 post-split, having peaked at about $0.30 in FY2024.▪ Stock compensation was $1,096.7m in FY2026, 22.8% of revenue and 104.8% of the entire non-GAAP operating profit, and it has risen as a share of revenue in each of the last two years and again in H1 FY2027, while Palo Alto, Zscaler, Fortinet and Okta each cut theirs. In FY2026 interest income of $195.0m exceeded free cash flow after stock compensation. Unrecognised stock compensation was $2,880m at July 31, 2026, up $822m in six months on a first-half grant count above the whole of FY2026.

4. The Q2 FY2027 print was a real step, and about a third of the FY2027 margin improvement is not operating leverage. Net new ARR of $332.8m beat the guided midpoint by 17%, grew 51% year over year, and holds up on a two-year stack at 24%. Against that, the FY2027 guided non-GAAP operating margin of 25.0% includes $85-95m from lengthening commission amortisation from four to five years ($53.4m realised in H1), worth about 1.5 points on the revenue guide▪, and FY2027 laps $44.8m of Strategic Plan restructuring plus most of $117.7m of FY2026 incident costs. Normalising H1 FY2027 for the commission change alone, the incremental non-GAAP operating margin is about 32% against a reported 41.3%, and the H1 margin is about 22.9% against a reported 24.4%.

5. ARR is the metric that sets management's pay, and it is under regulatory review. The cash bonus pays 70% on net new ARR. ARR is management-defined: contracts in active renewal negotiation stay in the number until the customer gives notice. In Q3 FY2025 about $26m was excluded from ARR after a federal-space distributor gave notice of transferability rights, while the revenue stayed in GAAP results. The 10-Q for the quarter ended April 30, 2025 first disclosed that the DOJ and the SEC "have requested information... relating to the Company's recognition of revenue and reporting of ARR for transactions with certain customers, the July 19 Incident and related matters", and the wording is unchanged across five consecutive filings. No accrual is recorded because no loss is estimable. The relevant precedent is SentinelOne's June 2023 ARR restatement of $27m, 5% of its ARR, which cost 35% of its market value in a session.

6. Falcon Flex has become the metric and the mechanism at the same time. Flex-adopted accounts held $2.29bn of ending ARR at July 2026, 39% of the total and up 101%, after 935 accounts were added in a single quarter. Conversion to Flex lifts an account's ending ARR by more than 40% on average, a first re-Flex adds 25% about eight months later, and accounts that have re-Flexed twice run 53% above their initial Flex. A re-Flex books expansion into current-period net new ARR ahead of the renewal date, so part of FY2027's step is renewal timing.▪ Management publishes the uplift percentages and not the ARR that would otherwise have arrived at renewal, and utilisation was last disclosed at above 75%, at Q2 FY2026. The 10-K states the other side: customers who cannot fully use their commitments may renew with shorter periods, fewer modules or smaller contract values.

7. Microsoft is simultaneously the largest competitor, the operating-system supplier and, from FY2027, a channel. IDC puts Microsoft first in modern endpoint security at 28.6% for CY2024, growing 28.2%; CrowdStrike's last self-published figure is 17.7% for the year to June 2022. Microsoft's Windows endpoint security platform, in private preview since July 2025 with CrowdStrike among eight partners, is designed to run endpoint protection in user mode, which would remove a source of outage risk for the whole industry and also remove the kernel-engineering barrier that has kept new entrants out. No general-availability date has been published, and Microsoft's stated position is that it "will continue to support third-party kernel mode drivers". Core Falcon ARR exposed to this is about $3.66bn, 63% of the total.

8. The cost base is being fixed ahead of the growth that fills it. Non-cancelable purchase commitments beyond one year went from $748m at January 2024 to $2,770m at January 2026 to $4,142m at July 2026, with a further $2.9bn signed after quarter-end running to FY2034, about $7.0bn in total against $5.0bn of cash. The FY2028 tranche alone is $843m, 14% of FY2027 guided revenue. Capex ran 9.5% of revenue in H1 FY2027 and 10.4% in Q2 against a 7-8% full-year guide, and data-centre equipment not yet in service rose 69% in six months to $274m. The counterparties and the take-or-pay terms are undisclosed, and the note bundles data-centre capacity with advertising, technology, equipment and consulting, so the composition cannot be tested from outside.

9. The professional-services line inflected the wrong way in the quarter everything else accelerated. Revenue grew 7% in Q2 FY2027 after 29% for FY2026 and 23% in Q1, and its GAAP gross margin was 10.3% against 17.9% for FY2026 and 33.1% two years earlier. The 10-Q attributes the margin decline to higher employee costs with no Strategic Plan offset and higher stock compensation. The 10-K calls the unit "a significant lead generator for new subscriptions" whose demand comes from breaches at non-customers, so a sustained slowdown here is an early signal on new-logo momentum; capacity constraints on scarce responders is the competing explanation, and the disclosures do not separate them.

10. Insider selling has been one-directional and heavy through the re-rating. Across 226 Form 4 filings from February 2025 to August 2026, eleven insiders sold about $619m of stock on the open market and none bought. Kurtz sold $290.6m, of which $86.5m in July and August 2026, including sales on the two days after the Q2 FY2027 print, under a plan adopted January 6, 2026. His beneficial ownership went from 16.3m shares (April 2021) to 2.4m (April 2026), and the board's answer was a $188.3m relative-total-return grant in December 2025 framed as retention. Related-party payments to Kurtz-controlled entities rose from $3.8m (FY2023) to $6.7m (FY2026) for aircraft, with a ten-year office lease from a Kurtz-owned entity beginning February 2027 at about $2m a year in rent and capital expenditure.

8. Management claim pressure tests

"The data moat creates a structural advantage no LLM provider can replicate" (Q4 FY2026 call). Engagement compounds: customers on six or more modules went from 24% (FY2021) to 51% (Q2 FY2027), and gross retention has held at 97-98% for six years. Share does not compound on the third-party measure available: IDC has Microsoft first at 28.6% for CY2024 growing 28.2%, and CrowdStrike's last self-published figure is 17.7% for the year to June 2022. And the effect has not shown up in price. The CFO says the company has "never been a company that has increased our prices to get more ARR"; the SIEM line is sold as "very disruptive from a price point"; and R&D was 28.8% of FY2026 revenue against 21.5% at Palo Alto and 12.0% at Fortinet. A data advantage that improves detection and retention without producing price increases or share gains against the largest rival is a real advantage of a bounded kind.▪

"Platform consolidation lowers the cost of growth." Net new ARR per dollar of the prior year's sales and marketing spend went from 1.70x (FY2022) to 1.34x, 0.97x, 0.71x and 0.66x (FY2026). The FY2027 guide midpoint implies 0.74x, the first improvement in five years and still below half the FY2022 level.▪ Sales and marketing grew 20% in FY2026 against 25% net new ARR growth, and 13% in H1 FY2027 against 42% net new ARR growth, so the recovery is in the numerator.

"Almost every new module is pure gross margin" (Fal.Con 2024). GAAP subscription gross margin was 78.0%, 77.8% and 77.7% in FY2024-FY2026 while the emerging trio went from 25% to 36% of ARR, and 77.8% in Q2 FY2027 against 77.1% a year earlier. Non-GAAP subscription gross margin reached 81% in Q2 FY2027, up about 90 basis points year over year on cloud optimisation. Hosting and data-centre depreciation were 42-44% of the increase in subscription cost of revenue in FY2026 and Q2 FY2027, capex is guided at 7-8% of revenue against 0.3% at Okta and Elastic, and SIEM retention is a storage cost. The incremental margin the claim predicts is a FY2029 target of 82-85% and has not appeared in a reported year.

"CrowdStrike is the leader in cloud security." Wiz reached more than $1bn of ARR at its March 2026 close with about 40% of the Fortune 100 [web] against CrowdStrike's more than $905m at July 2026. Both roughly doubled over two years. Wiz's latest-year growth is 43% on the source's own dated figures and 59-74% annualising from two points; CrowdStrike's is above 29%. Palo Alto claimed "the largest pure-play cybersecurity cloud security business being the first to $700 million in ARR" in August 2024, when CrowdStrike was above $515m. Each vendor's claim uses a different scope, and by ARR CrowdStrike is second or third among the pure-plays and behind Microsoft's Defender for Cloud, which passed $1bn of trailing revenue in June 2024.

"Next-Gen SIEM is a price disruptor" (Fal.Con 2025 deck, slide 61). CrowdStrike's per-gigabyte rate for third-party ingest is the highest of the scaled vendors, at roughly $2,170-2,680 per GB/day-year against $750-1,620 for Splunk and Sentinel at commitment tiers [web]. The disruption is in the billing base, not the rate: Falcon-generated data is not charged and every Insight customer gets 10 GB/day free. Microsoft applies the same structure with its own logs, and Palo Alto with firewall and Cortex data, so the mechanism is available to two of the three largest rivals and unavailable to Splunk and Elastic.▪

"Identity re-accelerated to 33-34%." The two named drivers are Falcon Shield, acquired November 2024 (+185% at Q2 FY2027, "more than 5x since our acquisition"), and privileged access, launched in FY2026 (+35x from a near-zero base). Kurtz also credits post-incident commitment-package renewals: identity "was a fan favorite in the days of CCP" (Q4 FY2026 call). The line was re-based in Q2 FY2026 to move Falcon Shield in from Cloud Security, growth rates were restated and levels apparently were not, so the FY2026 deceleration and the FY2027 re-acceleration are partly definitional. Organic identity growth cannot be pinned tighter than 20-33% [estimate: the 20% end assumes Shield and privileged access together supplied 40-50% of the roughly $150m twelve-month add; the 33% end is the printed rate].

"The July 19 incident is behind us." The commercial recovery is complete on the ARR evidence: net new ARR reached a record in Q2 FY2027 and gross retention never dropped below 97%. Three things are open. The DOJ and SEC information requests are unchanged across five filings. Incident costs continued into H1 FY2027 at $3.6m after $60.1m and $117.7m in the two prior years. And the commitment packages extended contract terms into FY2027-FY2028 renewals, with the 10-K stating that they "have resulted, and are expected to continue to result, in increased contraction, due to elongated subscription terms, and decreased upsell dollar values" while the Q4 FY2026 call describes the same accounts as having "gross and net retention rates higher than the company average" and having "already expanded more than twice the total $80 million of ARR value we provided". The two statements can both be true; the cohort's composition is undisclosed, so neither can be checked.

"Profitability is proven." Non-GAAP operating margin rose from 7.1% (FY2021) to 21.7% (FY2026) and a guided 25.0% for FY2027. GAAP operating income was negative in every quarter of FY2027 to date. Stock compensation was 25.6% of revenue in Q2 FY2027 and grew 35% against revenue growth of 26%. Interest income supplies about $152m of the FY2027 guided non-GAAP net income of $1,302.7-1,311.6m against operating income of $1,497.2-1,508.4m at a 21% assumed tax rate. Bloomberg's FY2027 GAAP EPS consensus was cut 77% over twenty-four months, from $0.46 to $0.105, while non-GAAP operating income estimates rose 10.4%. Two consensus snapshots taken on 2026-09-02 are used: Sections 13 and 15 run off the morning pull and Sections 14 and 17 off the evening pull. They differ on seven figures by rounding alone, among them FY2027 revenue of $6,003m against $6,004m and FY2027 non-GAAP operating income of $1,505m against $1,504m.

"The $10 billion ARR goal shows the runway." From the FY2027 guided exit of $6.61bn, $10bn by January 2031 needs a 10.9% compound rate, against 24% ARR growth in FY2026 and 26% guided for FY2027. Holding the FY2027 net new ARR guide flat and never raising it again delivers $10bn during FY2030. Every one of the six analysts who publishes an FY2031 revenue estimate implies more than $10bn of ending ARR, the lowest at about $11.0bn. The published goal is a legacy number set in September 2023 from a $2.9bn base, and it is below the current run-rate.

Candor. The response to the outage was direct on the facts: an apology opening the Q2 FY2025 call, a three-item remediation list, disclosure of "more than $60 million in deals that we had line of sight for the quarter", the sized commitment-package headwind, the withdrawal of the free-cash-flow target, and a forecast of acceleration "starting in the back half of next year" that proved right. Answers to competitive questions open by characterising rivals ("false narratives and misinformation from our competitors" on the kernel question, "FUD" on two earlier calls, "a made-up fugazi term" for platformization) before addressing the substance, which they then do at length. Concessions are framed as demand ("customers benefit because they get what they want, more Falcon"). And metrics are retired when they stop improving: the 5-or-more-module rate was dropped after Q4 FY2025 at 67%, the subscription-customer count after 29,000 for FY2024, the quarterly net retention figure after it first went below management's benchmark in Q2 FY2024, and the professional-services conversion ratio after FY2023, which spans the entire post-incident period.

Aug 26, 2026 Q2 FY2027: record net new ARR $332.8m (+51%), $47m above the top of guidance; shares +20.5% the next session, the largest one-day gain on record Fifth consecutive quarter of revenue acceleration

Four inflections.

Cash generation arrives, FY2020-FY2021. Ending ARR went 3.4x to $1,050m, non-GAAP operating margin from −46% to +7%, and free cash flow swung $358m to $292.9m, while net retention declined from 147% to 125% as the base grew. The mechanism was the single-agent architecture reaching the scale at which each added module cost little to serve; subscription gross margin went from 36% (FY2017) to 69% (FY2019) to 78% (Q1 FY2021). What management chose, under a demand windfall, was to spend: it raised full-year guidance in June 2020 while raising its own assumed churn, kept and increased the R&D hiring plan, gave product away to more than 250 customers, bought Preempt and Humio for $461m with under $11m of combined ARR while its own stock traded at 45-60x trailing sales, and issued $750m of eight-year notes at 3% with $1.1bn already in the bank.

The November 2022 reset and the pivot to margin, FY2023-FY2024. Revenue growth halved from 54% to 36% and net retention went 125% to 119%, while non-GAAP operating margin rose six points to 22% and GAAP net income turned positive for the first time. Management stopped adding headcount after a 46% expansion, moved to "enablement and productivity", extended payment terms, accepted more one-year renewals, and set a 30% free-cash-flow margin as the operating constraint. The stress was external; the margin step was chosen, with $2.7bn of cash available to keep hiring instead. By Q2 FY2024 the original target model was met a year early, and in September 2023 the target was raised by nine points of operating margin with Falcon Flex introduced.

The July 19, 2024 outage. Direct costs: $177.8m of incident expense net of insurance over two years, about $80m of ARR value in commitment packages, about $26m of federal-distributor ARR excluded, $73m of outage-related and $43m of payment-term cash effects concentrated in Q1 FY2026, and $44.8m of restructuring in May 2025. Indirect: net new ARR of $806.7m in FY2025 against $875.5m, a seven-point drop in net retention to 112%, and the open regulatory requests. The response was commercial concession and product bundling, with no layoffs for ten months. Two features became structural: Flex is now "how we go to market", and the ARR series now includes Flex re-expansions taken seven to eight months into a contract.

Flex-led re-acceleration and the AI demand step, H2 FY2026 to H1 FY2027. Net new ARR went from $221m (+1%) at the Q2 FY2026 trough to $330.7m (+47%) and $332.8m (+51%), Flex-adopted ARR reached $2.29bn, and the emerging lines passed $2bn. The demand shock was external; the commercial model that captured it was built during the 2024 crisis. Four items in the FY2027 prints are not organic: $7.8m of acquired net new ARR in Q1, the $53.4m of realised commission benefit in H1, the lapping of incident-depressed quarters, and re-Flex expansions booked "well ahead of their subscription renewal date" (Q1 FY2027 call).

Behavioural pattern. Under a demand windfall the company spends and raises long-range targets. Under a demand slowdown it slows hiring, protects free cash flow and gives customers time on payment terms and contract length. Under a self-inflicted crisis it concedes commercially and bundles. Against a competitive attack it cites third-party test results and platform breadth, and after the outage it partnered with the rival. When a metric stops improving it is retired or re-based and replaced with a broader one.

10. Management, incentives and capital allocation

10.1 Who runs the company

Three designated executive officers: George Kurtz (55, co-founder, CEO since November 2011, previously McAfee's worldwide CTO and founder of Foundstone), Burt Podbere (60, CFO since September 2015, the only CFO of the public company) and Michael Sentonas (52, President since March 2023, CTO from February 2020, at the company since 2016). The go-to-market, legal, HR and accounting leaders are not Section 16 officers. Shawn Henry, chief security officer from 2012, had his President of Services title removed in October 2022 and his bonus target cut from 100% to 50% of salary for FY2024, and retired to an advisory role on March 31, 2025. Global CTO Elia Zaitsev left on August 20, 2026, four trading days before the Q2 FY2027 print, to launch an AI-cybersecurity venture fund with two former CrowdStrike corporate-development executives. The shares declined 5.6% on the report and no successor was named [web, unverified]. On the Q2 FY2027 call Kurtz described the June 2026 appointment of Bartley Richardson as Chief AI and Autonomous Systems Officer as "part of our long planned and mutually agreed upon CTO leadership transition".

Governance is concentrated by design. Nine directors on a classified board with three-year terms; five of the eight independent directors have served eight to fifteen years. Kurtz chairs a Transaction Committee created in October 2023 "to review, evaluate and approve certain potential acquisitions" that held no meetings in FY2024, FY2025 or FY2026, the years in which Flow Security, Adaptive Shield, Onum and Pangea closed, with Seraphic and SGNL closing in Q1 FY2027. Supermajority provisions remain in the charter after stockholders rejected the board's request to ratify them at the June 17, 2026 meeting by 144.9m against to 24.0m for, 14.2% support. Say-on-pay is triennial, a frequency chosen in 2021 on the strength of Class B super-votes; the next vote is in 2027. Withhold votes against long-tenured directors have run 26-39%.

10.2 What the pay plan measures

FY2026 design: Kurtz's salary $1,100,000, bonus target 135% of salary, annual equity $50,000,000 (from $35,000,000), split half performance units and half time-vested units, plus a 300,000-unit relative-total-return award granted December 22, 2025 with a grant-date fair value of $188.3m. The cash bonus is measured and paid quarterly on 70% net new ARR and 30% non-GAAP operating income, with a net-retention modifier of plus or minus 10%. The performance units use revenue and non-GAAP EPS over a one-year performance period followed by four-year service vesting.

Metric Where Does it reward per-share value? Comment
Net new ARR (70% of bonus) Corporate Incentive Plan No; rewards size Counts acquired ARR; Flex re-expansions lift it without revenue; the $26m federal exclusion was a management judgement; the metric is under regulatory review
Non-GAAP operating income (30% of bonus) Corporate Incentive Plan Partly Excludes stock compensation, incident costs and restructuring; certified achievement runs 6-14 points above what the reported figure implies (below)
Net retention modifier Corporate Incentive Plan Quality of growth The band was re-set each year as the reported rate declined: 120% (FY2023-FY2024), 115-120% (FY2025), 110-115% (FY2026)
Revenue (50% of PSU) Annual PSU No; size One-year period; the range equals the company's own initial guidance
Non-GAAP EPS (50% of PSU) Annual PSU Per share, but blind to stock compensation and to $195m of interest income Excludes acquisition effects
Relative total return Dec 2025 award Yes CEO only; target payout at the 55th percentile

No plan uses free cash flow, GAAP profit, return on capital or share count, and every bonus and annual performance metric is measured over one year or one quarter, so the performance units function as time-vested units sized by one year's beat against guidance.

The performance-unit ranges have tracked the company's own guidance and then narrowed. In FY2024 and FY2025 the threshold equalled the low end of initial guidance and the target the high end. In FY2026 the target moved down to the guidance midpoint, the maximum down to the guidance high end, and the threshold payout doubled from 25% to 50%. FY2026 revenue of $4,812.1m came in $6.6m above the original guidance high end and paid the performance units at 200% of target; Kurtz's FY2026 total compensation was $247.6m, the largest in the company's history, and his annual package excluding the special award rose 43% in the incident-recovery year.

The profitability component does not reconcile to the reported figure:

Fiscal year Aggregate quarterly OI target Reported non-GAAP operating income Reported as % of target Certified achievement
FY2024 $715.6m $679.6m 95.0% 105.4%
FY2025 $886.5m $879.9m 99.3% 108.6%
FY2026 $1,146.4m $1,046.5m 91.3% 105.0%

On the reported figure the FY2026 profitability component would have paid about 64%, not 105%. Two explanations fit the arithmetic and neither appears in the proxy: the plan may measure operating income before the company-wide bonus accrual [estimate: the implied add-back is $75m, $83m and $157m for FY2024-FY2026], or each quarter's target may be set at the start of that quarter so that an average of quarterly achievement is not comparable to an annual sum. The FY2026 aggregate target of $1,146.4m also exceeds the initial FY2026 non-GAAP operating income guidance of $944.2-985.1m by 16%, which is possible only if later quarters' targets were set after guidance rose. The net-new-ARR certifications, by contrast, reconcile to the reported figures within a million dollars in each of the three years.

FY2025, the incident year, paid 106% of target in cash and 76% on performance units. The quarterly target-setting cadence allowed the second-half bar to be re-set after July 2024, and the plan definition excludes incident costs.

Management's stated ceiling, "less than 2% this year, strive to keep it under 3% in the years that are coming" (Q1 FY2024 call), was exceeded in FY2024 on both disclosed bases (2.4% weighted, 2.6% outstanding) and met in every year since.

10.5 Buybacks and the framework

The board authorised $1.0bn on June 3, 2025 and raised it to $1.5bn on April 6, 2026. No shares were repurchased in the eight months to January 2026, while the stock averaged $87.99-141.72. Every purchase was made inside the 37% drawdown from November 2025 to February 2026: 1,920k post-split shares for $175.6m at an average of $91.47, 11% below the quarter's average close and 7% above its low. No shares were bought in Q2 FY2027, when the stock averaged $171.60, and $1,324m of the authorisation was unused at July 31, 2026. The pace rose when the price declined and stopped when it rose, on a sample of one episode. The scale is small against every denominator: 0.19% of shares outstanding, 16% of six-month gross issuance, 26% of six-month stock compensation, and about five weeks of unit releases at the FY2026 rate.

Management's stated framework has never included a hurdle rate, a leverage target or a dilution-offset rule. The authorisation was tied to acquisitions in the same sentence that announced it: it "reflects our confidence in CrowdStrike's long-term strategy, including M&A, growth prospects and robust cash flow generation... We will continue to prioritize investing in our growth and innovation while retaining the flexibility to opportunistically repurchase shares" (Q1 FY2026 call). The quantified commitments are the capex ratio, the dilution ceiling and the FY2029 target model. Against that model, free cash flow margin has moved away from the target: 30.7% (FY2024), 26.9%, 25.7% (FY2026), 28.1% for the twelve months to July 2026, against a 34-38% FY2029 target and an at-least-30% FY2027 guide.▪

11. M&A, divestitures and deal track record

CrowdStrike has been a disciplined acquirer on every available outcome test, and the disclosures do not allow the most recent $1.5bn to be assessed.▪ Thirteen acquisitions since 2017 were private companies, bought mainly for cash, none larger than $637m of accounting consideration, none divested, none renegotiated, none blocked. No goodwill or intangible impairment has been recorded in any fiscal year (FY2026 10-K: "No impairment losses were recorded during the fiscal years ended January 31, 2026, January 31, 2025, or January 31, 2024"). There have been no divestitures since inception, no terminated signed agreements, no regulator-forced remedies, and one earn-out, on a $8.0m deal in 2017.

11.2 Deal outcomes

The two oldest large deals produced the outcome. Preempt at $91.2m for about $6.8m of ARR became a line above $585m; Humio at $370.3m plus a $57.2m tax charge for about $3.6m of ARR became a line above $695m.▪ Both lines include product built in-house on the acquired base, so the purchases' own share is undisclosed, and $461m of consideration became two lines exceeding $1.28bn of ending ARR five to six years later.

Three limits apply. The impairment test cannot fail: CrowdStrike is a single reporting unit, so $2,251m of goodwill is tested against a company fair value near $210bn, and a $60m tuck-in that produced nothing would never register. SecureCircle, at $60.6m, has no disclosed data-protection ARR and the product was rebuilt in-house. Second, no acquisition after Humio has had its own ARR disclosed, and product-line ARR is re-based, so the return on the $1.7bn spent since September 2023 is not measurable from outside. Third, the price per dollar of acquired ARR is not a value test because the company buys products before they have revenue: Humio cost about 100x its acquired ARR and SGNL plus Seraphic about 130x [estimate: consideration divided by the disclosed acquired net new ARR, which excludes contracts management did not count as recurring at close, so these are maximums].

The economic price is above the accounting price in every deal. Across the nine deals with a reported headline the gap is about $0.4-0.5bn [estimate: sum of press headline less ASC 805 consideration], from two causes the filings state: replacement equity that vests after closing is compensation and is expensed as stock-based compensation, and the accounting figure is net of cash acquired while the headline is not ($25.7m at Bionic, $13.7m at Adaptive Shield, $12.5m at Humio). A founder-holdback obligation of $45.4m at January 31, 2026, a fixed dollar amount settled in a variable number of shares contingent on continued employment, is outside the equity tables. Non-GAAP operating margin excludes all of it.

Management's stated criterion has been consistent for six years and is a preference, not a rule: "It's got to be great tech and great people. If it has ARR, so be it. But the first two are the key" (Barclays, 2021-12-08); "we love great teams. We love great technologies, and it's even better if they have no go-to-market because we don't have to pay for that" (Morgan Stanley, 2023-03-09); "we're not looking to buy ARR" (April 2023 briefing). What has changed is size. In September 2020 the CFO said "We wouldn't be going out there and buying $1 billion company. That's more unlikely" (Citi conference); SGNL's headline was $740m five years later, and in March 2026 the CFO described the cash balance as something that "isn't sitting in the bank getting whatever 3%, 4%" and said a transformational deal would have to be "a deal of the century".

Integration precedes selling, consistently. Preempt's agent was rewritten into the Falcon sensor; Humio was relaunched as LogScale eighteen months after close; Pangea was "really starting to sell that in Q4 because we wanted to take the time and effort to integrate it" (Q3 FY2026 call); SGNL and Seraphic are guided to "minimal organic contribution" in FY2027 while their capabilities are natively integrated. Integration costs money: FY2027 non-GAAP guidance includes $74-80m of integration operating expense for the four latest deals, against the $85-95m commission-amortisation benefit, and acquisition-related expenses excluded from non-GAAP results were $14.2m in H1 FY2027, matching all of FY2026.

One approach did not proceed: in August 2024 Action1, a patch-management vendor, said it had received an approach reported at about $1bn and would stay founder-led, while CrowdStrike's corporate-development head described a single 45-minute conversation [web].

CrowdStrike has one debt instrument and is otherwise funded by customer prepayments.

Weighted-average cost of debt: with a single fixed-rate instrument, the principal-weighted coupon is 3.00%. Cash interest is $22.5m a year; the effective rate including issuance-cost amortisation is 3.2% ($24.0m of notes-related interest expense in FY2026). Income-statement interest expense of $28.0m in FY2026 also included amortisation of revolver fees, which stopped when the facility expired.

The notes are rated Baa2 by Moody's and BBB- by S&P (stable, rating dated 2026-06-16); Fitch does not rate them, so the indenture's covenant-suspension test, which requires investment grade from all three agencies, is not met and the covenants on liens, subsidiary guarantees, dividends and asset sales still apply. The bond traded at 95.21 on 2026-09-02 at a 5.10% yield to maturity and an 83 basis-point Z-spread. Refinancing $750m at that yield would cost about $38m a year, $16m more than the current coupon, 1.3% of FY2026 free cash flow; the notes are callable at par now and cash is 6.7x the principal, so the maturity is a choice. Non-GAAP operating income of $1,046m covers the cash coupon 47x; GAAP coverage is negative for FY2026 and positive in both quarters of FY2027 to date. Interest income of $195.0m in FY2026 was 7x interest expense, and is guided down to $160-170m for FY2027 as cash is deployed.

A $750m facility put in place in January 2021 alongside the notes was never drawn and expired on January 2, 2026 without replacement, leaving no committed bank liquidity. The CFO's account of the January 2021 financing (Needham conference, 2021-01-14) was that the company judged itself "wildly under leveraged", chose a high-yield bond for "no dilution to our shareholders", and treated the debut as an introduction to the rating agencies so that a larger bond could fund a multi-billion acquisition "2, 3, 4 years out". Five years on, the notes have moved to investment grade at both rating agencies and no further debt has been raised.

Leases, pension and other obligations. Operating leases are $74.0m of present value at July 31, 2026 on a 4.7-year weighted term at a 5.3% discount rate, with $117.5m of undiscounted payments on four leases signed but not commenced (starting October 2026 to August 2027). There are no finance leases and no pension or post-retirement obligation. Other items: $69.7m of unfunded customer-financing commitments through CrowdStrike Financial Services, a $45.4m founder-holdback obligation settled in a variable number of shares, $140.9m of gross unrecognised tax benefits, and a $13.1m July 19 incident accrual.

Liquidity. Cash and equivalents of $5,014m at July 31, 2026 with no short-term investments and $163m of restricted cash in escrows, against $750m of notes. Cash is held in money-market funds, Treasury bills and time deposits. The six-month decline of $138m reflects $881m of acquisitions, $176m of buybacks and $25m of distributions to the Falcon Funds' outside investors against the operating inflow. The first hedging programme began in Q2 FY2027: $57.9m notional of foreign-currency forwards with maturities of three months or less. Nearly all sales contracts are denominated in dollars, so the exposure is on non-dollar operating expenses in sterling, Australian dollars, euros, Canadian dollars and rupees.

Ten-year capital structure. Pre-IPO the company was funded by preferred stock, with a stockholders' deficit of $(487.8)m at January 2019 and $557.9m of preferred in mezzanine. The June 2019 IPO raised $659.2m net on 20,700k Class A shares and converted 131,268k preferred shares to Class B. The January 2021 notes were the only debt event. All Class B shares converted automatically on December 11, 2024. Net cash went from $912m (FY2020) to $4,485m (FY2026) and $4,264m at July 2026; net debt to EBITDA excluding stock compensation has been between (3.5)x and (12.1)x since FY2021, negative because the company is in net cash.

Share count grew 3.1%, 2.2%, 2.6%, 2.5% and 2.2% in FY2022-FY2026, a 2.9% compound rate from FY2020. In H1 FY2027 the company issued 12,312k post-split shares (1.21% of opening) and repurchased 1,920k (0.19%), ending at 1,023,845k, up 1.03% in six months. Weighted diluted shares were 1,044,469k in Q2 FY2027 against 1,019,448k basic, so 25.0m of dilutive equivalents (2.5%) are outside the basic count. The employee stock purchase plan sells at 85% of the lower of the offering-start or purchase-date price with a 24-month look-back: 440k pre-split shares were issued in FY2026 for $125.8m, about $286 a share against a $453 pre-split average price [estimate: proceeds divided by shares issued; the discount arises from the look-back to the 2024 offering start].

The company holds federal net operating losses of $2.6bn with indefinite life, $417.4m of California and $998.3m of other state losses, $84.2m in the UK and $227.0m of federal research credits, all behind a full valuation allowance. They reduce cash taxes when GAAP profits return; the 21% non-GAAP tax rate is an assumption and not a cash rate.

Structural risks, ordered by the size of the obligation against FY2026 free cash flow of $1,236m. Non-cancelable purchase commitments of about $7.0bn including the post-quarter signing, 5.7x free cash flow, with the FY2028 tranche at $843m and the counterparties and take-or-pay terms undisclosed; the exposure is to the gross margin. Stock compensation and dilution, at $2.9bn of unrecognised expense (2.3x free cash flow) with buybacks so far offsetting 16% of issuance. Litigation and regulation, where the Delta suit is in discovery, the DOJ and SEC requests are open, no loss range is estimable and $13.1m is accrued. No committed bank liquidity after the revolver expired. A single $750m maturity in February 2029, 0.6x free cash flow, callable at par. Structural subordination is minimal, because the guarantor group held $2,855m of the $2,856m of H1 FY2027 revenue. There is no floating-rate debt and no currency mismatch on debt or revenue.

13.3 What drove growth, margin and cash

Revenue. Subscription revenue compounded at 70% a year from FY2017 to FY2026 and professional services at 37%, so services declined from 28.2% of revenue to 5.1%. Non-US revenue went from 16.5% of the total in FY2018 to 33.2% in FY2026, with most of the shift in the first four years and about one point a year since FY2022. Price against volume cannot be separated: the pricing units themselves changed, and the only volume proxy that ran for more than a few years, the subscription-customer count, stops at FY2024 at 29,000. Over the seven years it ran, ARR per subscription customer moved from $124k (FY2019) to $106k (FY2021 and FY2022) and back to $118k (FY2024); the decline is the move down-market into Falcon Go and MSSP-served accounts and the recovery is module expansion. Dollar-based net retention measures expansion directly: 147% (FY2019), 124-125% through FY2023, then 119%, 112% and 115%.

Organic against acquired. CrowdStrike does not separate acquired ARR, and three disclosures exist in ten years: $6.8m of FY2021 net new ARR from Preempt, $4.5m of FY2022 from Humio and SecureCircle, and $7.8m of Q1 FY2027 from SGNL and Seraphic. Against FY2022 net new ARR of $681.3m, the disclosed acquired portion was 0.7%. Cash spent tells a different story about where capital went, from $6.5m in FY2018 to $881.4m in H1 FY2027 alone. Currency is not a revenue variable: nearly all contracts are in dollars and the exposure is on non-dollar operating expenses.

Gross margin. From 35.5% (FY2017) to 74.7% (FY2026), and flat in a 73-75% band since FY2021. The subscription line does the work and has itself been flat at 76-78% for six years.▪ Services gross margin declined from 33.4% (FY2022) to 19.0% (FY2025), 17.9% (FY2026) and 10.3% in Q2 FY2027; had services held its FY2024 31.8% margin, FY2026 gross profit would have been $34.4m higher, worth 0.7 of a point of consolidated gross margin.▪ And FY2026 subscription cost rose on the six items listed in Section 1.1, of which hosting and data-centre depreciation were 44%.

Operating margin. GAAP moved from (171.7)% to (6.1)% and non-monotonically: the best year was FY2024 at (0.6)%, and FY2025 and FY2026 went backwards. The FY2026 bridge against FY2025:

Component $m
Revenue +858
Cost of revenue (229)
Gross profit +630
Sales and marketing (308)
Research and development (309)
General and administrative (189)
Change in operating income (177)
of which higher stock compensation (235)
of which Strategic Plan restructuring, new in FY2026 (45)
of which incremental July 19 incident costs, net of insurance (58)
Residual: operating income excluding those three +161

On $858m of incremental revenue the underlying operating result improved by $161m, a 19% incremental margin, and all of the reported deterioration came from stock compensation, the restructuring and the incident. The operating ratios show where the leverage stopped: sales and marketing declined from 87.8% of revenue (FY2018) to 37.3% (FY2024) and then rose to 38.5% and 38.1%; research and development bottomed at 24.5% in FY2021 and has risen every year since to 28.8%; general and administrative bottomed at 12.2% in FY2025 and rose to 13.9% on incident legal costs. Sales and marketing at 35.0% of H1 FY2027 revenue against 39.0% a year earlier is the line that moved in FY2027, and part of that is the commission-amortisation change.

Below the operating line, interest income has become material: nil before FY2022, then $3.8m, $52.5m, $148.9m, $196.2m and $195.0m. In FY2024 it converted a $19.1m operating loss into $105.7m of pre-tax income. The guided FY2027 range is $160-170m, so the support is shrinking as cash is deployed. The tax provision has been positive in both loss and profit years, at $72.4m in FY2022 and $71.1m in FY2025, because a full valuation allowance applies to US deferred tax assets and the provision is foreign and state tax on profitable subsidiaries.

Cash conversion. Free cash flow has exceeded EBITDA excluding stock compensation in every year since FY2021, at 301%, 187%, 157%, 121%, 111% and 114%, because deferred revenue grows faster than the profit-and-loss account. Against non-GAAP net income the multiple compressed from 7.06x (FY2022) to 1.29x (FY2026). Days sales outstanding has been 100-104 for five years, long for software and a function of annual up-front billing concentrated in the January quarter; the allowance for credit losses was $3.0m against $1,362m of gross receivables at January 2026. Deferred revenue is 361 days of revenue, down from 489 in FY2018 as multi-year prepayment mixed down and remaining performance obligations took its place, with RPO to ending ARR rising from 1.27x to 1.71x and to 1.83x at July 2026.

Net new ARR growth went from +25% for FY2026 to +32% and +51%, and survives the two-year test at 24%; the FY2027 net new ARR guide was raised twice for a cumulative $116m and 1,150 basis points of growth. Revenue growth accelerated for a fifth consecutive quarter, and subscription revenue at +27.0% now runs above ARR growth of 25.4%, which reverses the customer-commitment-package separation and cannot continue indefinitely. Non-GAAP operating margin went from 21.7% to 25.3%, of which about 1.5 points on a full-year basis is the commission-amortisation change and the rest laps the incident and restructuring costs. Capital intensity moved the other way: capex was 7.7% of FY2026 revenue against 9.5% in H1 FY2027 and 10.4% in Q2 alone, with purchases of property and equipment of $124.4m in the quarter against $30.5m a year earlier, the highest quarterly figure since FY2023. Stock compensation including employer payroll taxes was 23.9% of FY2026 revenue and 27.1% in Q2 FY2027 alone. And professional services gross margin at 10.3% is the lowest print in the company's public history, on 7% revenue growth, while the same call described "an all-time record $71 million" of services revenue; both statements are true, and the growth rate does not support the demand claim.

Dollar-based net retention has been described as "improved sequentially" in both FY2027 quarters and given as a figure exactly once since Q2 FY2024, in the Q3 FY2025 10-Q.

Management's own delivery record is why the current-year consensus contains so little information. Revenue exceeded the guided midpoint in 21 of 22 quarters and exceeded the top of the range in 21 of 22; non-GAAP operating income exceeded the top of the guided range in 22 of 22; non-GAAP EPS met or beat the Bloomberg estimate in 29 of the 30 quarters since the IPO.
