The guided range narrowed at the same time, from 1.5% of the midpoint for Q1 FY2022 revenue to 0.29% for Q1 FY2027. On the annual guide, the initial cushion declined from +11.1% (FY2020) and +14.0% (FY2021) to +2.4% (FY2024), −0.1% (FY2025) and +0.8% (FY2026), so a guide set today embeds roughly a tenth of the conservatism the FY2021 guide did.

ARR, the newest guided metric, was guided loosely. Q2 FY2027 ending ARR was guided in a $2m band on a $5.79bn base and came in $46.8m above the top, and the implied net new ARR range of $284-286m was cleared by 17%. That is the largest percentage beat on any guided metric since Q4 FY2025, and it arrived one quarter after ARR guidance began.

Where consensus is doing work. FY2027 is settled: 47 EPS contributors spanning $1.21 to $1.28. FY2028 is where views appear: the revenue range widens to 7.2% of the mean and the EPS range to 35.1%. FY2029 has 27 revenue contributors and a 21.4% range. FY2030 has five and FY2031 six, with an FY2031 revenue range of $10,018m to $18,554m, so the long-range "consensus" is five or six models. Two operating-income lows in the pool (FY2028 at $341m against a $1,918m mean, FY2029 at $776m against $2,473m) are consistent with GAAP submissions pooled into a non-GAAP mean, so the published lows on that line are unusable.

The price has moved on the multiple, not the estimates. Over the twelve months to 2026-09-02 the shares rose 99% while FY2027 revenue estimates rose 2.9%, FY2027 non-GAAP EPS 5.4% and FY2028 revenue 3.5%.▪ The estimate contribution to that return is roughly five points. Working the other way, FY2027 GAAP EPS consensus was cut 77% over twenty-four months, from $0.46 to $0.105, and FY2028 from $0.51 to $0.256, as stock compensation and acquisition amortisation grew faster than revenue.

Analysts' questions on the calls have changed twice in six months. In March 2026, with the stock eight days off its low, Kurtz opened the Q4 FY2026 call with "The market is questioning enterprise software's role in an agentic world" and analysts asked him to defend the moat against frontier labs. In June 2026 the question inverted to whether the new AI-driven demand is durable, with one analyst calling it "a bit of panic spending" and another pressing that the inflection "seems like that's more about interest and intent". In August 2026, thirteen analysts asked thirteen questions and none was about the guide, the margin, the GAAP-to-non-GAAP gap, Microsoft, or the regulatory requests.

This section records what the market paid and what it reacted to, with no valuation judgment.

The 2021-2023 decline began with the rate-driven de-rating of unprofitable software and was confirmed by the company's own numbers on 2022-11-29, when Q3 FY2023 net new ARR of $198.1m grew 17%, small-business days-to-close lengthened by 11, about $10m of ARR was deferred by phased start dates, and Q4 net new ARR was guided down by up to 10% sequentially. The shares declined 14.7% the next session. Forward estimates barely moved and the multiple did all the work: the twelve-month-forward consensus P/E went from 409x at the November 2021 peak to 52x at the FY2023 close while forward EPS rose from $0.179 to $0.505.

The 2024 outage decline of 44% ran far ahead of any estimate change. Forward consensus EPS was $1.107 on 2024-07-18 and still $1.089 on 2024-08-27, a cut of 1.6%. The estimate damage arrived seven months later: the Q4 FY2025 print of 2025-03-04 delivered a 20.3% EPS beat and guided FY2026 non-GAAP EPS to $3.33-3.45 against the $3.93 just reported, and forward consensus EPS was cut from $1.118 to $0.882 in two sessions, the largest two-session cut in the daily series since 2021.

The November 2025 to February 2026 decline of 37% was a sell-off across application software on concern that AI agents would displace enterprise software; no CrowdStrike-specific estimate cut accompanied it and forward EPS kept rising through the drawdown. The 164% recovery from that low to the August 31 close of $231.00 came in two steps: the April 2026 "Mythos moment", worth 64% between the February low and late May, and the Q2 FY2027 print, which added 20.5% in one session, the largest single-day gain on record.

Both directions are set by the guide and by net new ARR, not by the print.

Dispersion widens sharply with horizon. FY2027 has 47 estimates spanning $1.21 to $1.28 with a standard deviation of $0.009. FY2029 has 26 spanning $1.85 to $2.61. FY2030 has six estimates and a $0.51 standard deviation on a $2.68 mean, so the 61-96x range it produces contains little information. Estimates have been rising and the revision came in the last month: the FY2027 EPS mean is up $0.040 over three months and $0.048 over four weeks, and FY2029 up $0.159 and $0.233. Company guidance issued on 2026-08-26 is revenue of $5,991-6,011m, non-GAAP operating income of $1,497-1,508m, non-GAAP EPS of $1.25-1.26, ending ARR of $6,603-6,612m and a free cash flow margin of at least 30%; consensus FY2027 is inside every one of those ranges.

Other dated reference points on 2026-09-02: trailing twelve-month EV/revenue 38x, price to book 41x, a Bloomberg consensus rating of 4.39 of 5 across 56 analysts (41 buy, 14 hold, 1 sell), a mean target price of $235.66, 90-day volatility of 64.3, adjusted beta 1.42 and short interest of 2.4% of float. The rating and target are those analysts' views, aggregated by Bloomberg.

The fiscal-year-to-date gain of 86% is mostly multiple expansion: twelve-month-forward consensus EPS rose 21% from $1.201 to $1.456 while the forward P/E rose 54% from 92x to 141x, so about three-quarters of the return came from the multiple [estimate: 69% on a log decomposition, 75% on the simple residual]. Over the longer window from the January 2023 trough the split is closer to even; from the November 2021 peak the multiple contracted by two-thirds while the company grew into the price.

17. Forward model summary

The model forecasts annual recurring revenue by product line as units multiplied by realized price, converts ARR to subscription revenue with a calibrated relationship, and models professional services separately. Year 0 is FY2026 and ties to the reported statements; the first two quarters of FY2027 are actual, so FY2027 is half reported. It runs to FY2036 and contains no valuation, no multiple and no discounting.

Because units and realized price are estimated jointly from a known ARR total, the product of the two is fixed and the split between them is not. Every scenario therefore moves both terms, and the sensitivity table separates them.

Starting units and prices at January 2026 (each pair reproduces the disclosed line ARR):

Line Unit Units Realized price ARR
Core Falcon platform protected endpoint-year 30.0m [estimate: midpoint of the 20-40m range in §1.5] $111.60 [estimate: core residual ARR over the unit count] $3,348m [estimate: total ARR less the three product-line minimums]
Cloud Security paid cloud workload-year 16.0m [estimate: line ARR over the assumed price] $50.00 [estimate: midpoint of the $34-114 committed list range] $800m
Next-Gen Identity protected identity-year 17.0m [estimate: line ARR over the assumed price] $30.59 [estimate: inside the $20-55 range in §1.4] $520m
Next-Gen SIEM GB/day of paid third-party ingest 308k [estimate: line ARR over the assumed price] $1,900 [estimate: below the $2,170-2,680 list and pay-as-you-go rates, allowing for commitment discount] $585m
Total $5,253m

ARR converts to subscription revenue as beginning ARR plus 0.338 of the year's net new ARR, calibrated on FY2024-FY2026 and set to reproduce the FY2027 guide. Costs are modelled as non-GAAP ratios, because that is the basis management steers and the FY2029 target model uses, and bridged to GAAP by adding stock compensation, employer payroll taxes, acquired-intangible amortisation and acquisition items, with stock compensation as its own driver so the GAAP gap stays explicit.

17.2 Assumptions and where each is contested

Bear and bull are deltas on named drivers. Ten-year averages shown.

Driver Basis Bear Base Bull The case against the base
Protected endpoints, FY2028-FY2036 growth Historical record 5.1%/yr 7.8%/yr 10.3%/yr Combined with the price driver this grows core ARR about 11% a year to $6,695m by FY2031, 34-91% above the $3.5-5.0bn core residual implied by management's own $10bn FY2031 composition. Microsoft's IDC share went 16.4% to 28.6% while CrowdStrike's last published figure stayed at 17.7%, and its user-mode Windows platform has been in preview since July 2025 with no general-availability date. The bear at 5.06% produces a 13.3% five-year company revenue CAGR, the 27th percentile of the reference class, so the left tail is thin
Core ARR per endpoint (module attach) Analyst judgment 1.3%/yr 3.0%/yr 4.3%/yr The attach metric management still publishes is flattening: six-plus-module adoption went 48% to 50% to 51% over eighteen months, and the 5-plus series was retired at 67%. Falcon Go at $59.99, MSSP wholesale at an implied $16-30 and about $80m of commitment-package ARR value all pull realized price down. The starting $111.60 is derived from a residual that is a maximum, so the whole compounded path inherits an upward bias
Cloud paid workloads Historical record 8.7%/yr 13.3%/yr 19.4%/yr The strongest attack is Wiz above $1bn of ARR inside Google with roughly 40% of the Fortune 100, and it fails on this driver: the base already has the annual dollar add declining from $230m to $110m, reaching $1,743m of cloud ARR at FY2031, $757m-$1,257m below management's own range and close to what a flat $205m add would produce
Realized cloud price Analyst judgment (4.2)%/yr (1.5)%/yr 0.0%/yr No scenario allows a cloud price increase across ten years, while identity gets +2.0% in the base and +0.2% even in the bear, and nothing in the sources distinguishes the two lines that way. The two price angles disagree by 2-6x, and the contractual workload definition alone moves the billed count 30-60%, so the scenario band is narrower than the identification range of its own starting level
Identity protected identities Historical record 9.5%/yr 14.0%/yr 18.8%/yr Two of the four named growth sources were bought, and the series was re-based in Q2 FY2026 by an undisclosed amount with no like-for-like rate given, so a ten-year 14.0% has never been observed organically. Working the other way, twelve-month dollar adds rose from about $85m to about $150m, attach was only about 4,000 identity customers against 29,000 subscription customers, and the base's FY2031 identity ARR of $1,407m is inside management's own $1.0-1.5bn range
Realized price per identity Analyst judgment +0.2%/yr +2.0%/yr — The sole evidence is an ASP uplift "north of 30%" quoted in August 2022, four years stale. Identity is the most bundled of the three lines, with Entra inside E5 and E7, Okta at the directory and CyberArk being absorbed into Palo Alto. Giving the most bundled line the only positive price path in the model, with a bear floor at zero, is the least supported price assumption in the set
SIEM paid third-party ingest Historical record 14.4%/yr 20.0%/yr 27.0%/yr Compounding volume at 20% for a decade assumes ten years of displacement against Cisco's Splunk and Microsoft's Sentinel at an unchanged 1.5-3x per-gigabyte premium, and Onum pipeline filtering, which management sells as a customer benefit, reduces billed volume, and the volume driver does not include it. The level survives: dollar adds rose from about $210m to about $265m, FY2027 unit growth of 48% is below the 60%-plus just printed, and FY2031 SIEM ARR of $1,954m is at the top of management's range without exceeding it
Realized SIEM price Analyst judgment (3.3)%/yr (1.3)%/yr +0.7%/yr Ten years at (1.3)% closes about 12% of a premium that runs 100-200% over the two largest alternatives, and any contested displacement closes more than that. Both supporting angles are list or pay-as-you-go rate cards, not realized prices, divided into a volume estimate that itself spans 1.8 times
ARR-to-revenue conversion Historical record 0.330 0.338 0.346 Solving the model's own identity on the three calibration years gives 0.3551 (FY2024), 0.4045 (FY2025) and 0.3194 (FY2026). The assumed band excludes all three, including the most recent year, which is below the bear. FY2025 is distorted by the commitment packages; FY2024 and FY2026 are not, and they straddle the band on both sides. The observed range is worth about plus or minus $65m of FY2027 revenue
Non-GAAP subscription cost Mgmt guidance 19.9% of sub. rev 18.3% 17.1% GAAP subscription gross margin has not expanded in three years (78.0%, 77.8%, 77.7%, 77.8% in Q2 FY2027) while purchase commitments went from $748m to about $7.0bn and capex ran 9.5% of revenue in H1 FY2027 against a 7-8% guide. Mix is shifting toward Next-Gen SIEM, which bills per gigabyte with 13-month retention and which the model assumes at a 92% non-GAAP gross margin, while Splunk and Elastic run low-to-mid-seventies cloud gross margins on the same workload. The base asks only 0.13 of a point a year and reaches the bottom of management's FY2029 band four years after that date
Non-GAAP sales and marketing Mgmt guidance 31.6% of rev 28.8% 27.5% GAAP sales and marketing stopped declining three years ago at 37-38.5% of revenue. FY2027's step to 29.0% is largely the commission-amortisation change, worth 1.4-1.6% of the revenue guide, which is not selling leverage; and the same change raises the capitalised commission balance while the model lowers the deferred-cost build from 25.2% of net new ARR to 22.0%
Non-GAAP research and development Mgmt guidance — 19.0% of rev — Holds. GAAP R&D has risen as a share of revenue for three years, but the entire gap between the rising GAAP ratio and the flat non-GAAP ratio is stock compensation, which is a separate driver. The base reproduces the reported non-GAAP ratio of about 19.5% in both H1 FY2026 and H1 FY2027 and declines 0.1 of a point a year from there, staying at the top of management's 15-20% band
Non-GAAP general and administrative Mgmt guidance — 5.05% of rev — The base settles at the bottom of management's 5-7% band for ten years while three open-ended costs land in this line: the DOJ and SEC requests with no disclosed scope; $74-80m of FY2027 integration expense against $642.6m a year of assumed further acquisitions; and GAAP general and administrative rising from 12.2% to 13.9% of revenue in FY2026
Stock compensation Base rate 22.2% of rev 19.1% 16.7% Attacked from both sides. Against the record: the ratio rose in seven of nine years and in each of the last three, to 23.6% in H1 FY2027, with $2,880m of unrecognised expense at July 2026, up $822m in six months. The bear only holds the FY2026 level and does not allow it to keep rising. Against the class: the median is 18.4% at the gate and 9.5% past $8bn of revenue, with Fortinet at 4.1% and Palo Alto at 14.0%, and the bull at 16.7% never reaches the class median
Capex Mgmt guidance 9.1% of rev 7.4% 6.6% H1 FY2027 ran 9.5% and Q2 alone 10.4%. Meeting the base's FY2027 figure needs H2 intensity to fall, which has not happened in either of the last two years. From FY2031 the model sets capex equal to depreciation, collapsing two assumptions into one, against a realized capex-to-D&A of 1.32x to 2.82x every year since FY2021
Depreciation and amortisation Historical record — 6.9% of rev 6.1% The bull requires D&A intensity below the FY2027 modelled level while roughly $7.0bn of contracted capacity is placed in service and depreciated over three to five years. The direction is sound: D&A plus intangible amortisation went 4.75% of revenue (FY2024) to 5.85% (FY2026)
Acquired-intangible amortisation Analyst judgment — $105.9m/yr flat — A flat ten-year constant between two diverging paths. Net intangibles went from about $140m to about $275m in six months against $1.17bn of consideration, which on a five-year life supports roughly $58m a year; the model's own $642.6m a year of assumed acquisitions supports roughly $155m a year in the back half. The line should be a function of the acquisition driver
Deferred revenue Historical record 321 days 346 days 355 days The most recent annual observation moved the other way: 344.2 days (FY2025) to 360.6 (FY2026), because deferred revenue grew 27.5% against revenue growth of 21.7%. The base takes about 2.5 days a year out for a decade on a mechanism that produced the opposite result in the year it was measured. RPO went $9.0bn to $10.7bn while the share due within twelve months went 51% to 46%; longer contracts billed annually raise days and the same duration in unbilled backlog lowers them, and the model assumes the second
Days sales outstanding Historical record 108 103 — Holds, and is the best-supported assumption in the set. DSO drifted 11 days over five years, the last four annual figures are within a 2.3-day range, the base is inside that range, and no year in the public record has exceeded 104.2
Deferred contract acquisition costs Historical record 27.7% of net new ARR 22.0% 20.1% Realized ratios are 15.4% (FY2024), 32.9% (FY2025) and 25.2% (FY2026), a three-year mean of 24.5%. The base is below both the mean and the most recent year, in a forecast whose first year contains the commission change that mechanically raises it, and the model takes the profit-and-loss benefit of that change in the sales-and-marketing ratio and the cash benefit here
Cash yield Analyst judgment 2.8% 3.09% 3.4% A band of plus or minus 0.3 points across ten years of short-term rates is narrower than a single central-bank move, and the company realized 4.08% in FY2026 and near zero in FY2021-FY2022. The larger problem is the balance it is applied to: the base accumulates $30.7bn of cash by FY2036, 1.7x that year's revenue, generating $884.5m of interest income, about 17% of that year's non-GAAP operating income, a ratio no member of the reference class has held
Diluted share growth Historical record — +1.68%/yr — Realized net growth was 2.6%, 4.5%, 0.5% and 2.4% in FY2023-FY2026, with FY2027 guided at 4.2%. The base decays from 1.80% to 1.00%, below every year in the record, while gross employee issuance has run 2.2-2.6% with no sign of slowing. Getting from 2.4% gross to 1.0% net needs the buyback to absorb well over half of issuance every year, against a total buyback history of $176m
GAAP effective tax rate Analyst judgment 22% 20% 19% CrowdStrike has reported positive pre-tax income in exactly two fiscal years and neither produced a rate inside the band: 30.5% in FY2024 and 121.5% in FY2025. A full valuation allowance still stands behind $2.6bn of federal net operating losses and $227.0m of research credits, and the model books no release, so it shows neither the one-time benefit nor any transition year above 22%
Cash acquisitions Historical record $777.6m/yr $642.6m/yr $552.6m/yr The entire assumed range is below what has already been spent. CrowdStrike paid $881m net of cash acquired for Seraphic and SGNL in H1 FY2027 alone, against a $777.6m high case for the full year, and $1,264m over the twelve months to July 2026, 63% of operating cash flow against a ten-year average of 24%. XM Cyber's assets, at $145m plus further shares, are expected to close in H2 FY2027 on top of that. The consequence is not confined to this line: understated acquisition spending inflates the cash balance, which inflates interest income, which inflates non-GAAP net income and EPS in every forecast year. The evidence supports $1.0-1.3bn for FY2027 and a base above $800m a year thereafter
Share repurchases Analyst judgment $287.6m/yr $587.6m/yr $1,008m/yr Total repurchases in the company's history are $176m, all inside a single 37% drawdown, and $1,324m of the authorisation was unused at July 2026. The base's ten-year spend of $5.9bn is 3.9x the authorisation outstanding and the bull's $10.1bn is 6.7x it. Revealed preference runs the other way: $1,264m on acquisitions against $176m on buybacks in the twelve months to July 2026

The bear does not break FY2027, because H1 is reported and Q3 is guided within a $6m band; bear FY2027 revenue of $5,953m is 0.6% below the low end of the standing guide, which would be the first full-year revenue shortfall against a standing guide in the company's public history. The bear's damage lands in FY2028 and after: net new ARR declines from $1,274m to $904m and then to $617m, non-GAAP operating margin returns to 19.7% against 21.7% in FY2026, and GAAP operating income stays negative through FY2036 because stock compensation holds at 21-22% of a slower-growing revenue base. The bull reaches management's 28-32% non-GAAP operating margin band in FY2029 and its 34-38% free-cash-flow band in FY2028.

17.4 Checks

Against the guide and consensus for FY2027: the base is inside both on revenue ($6,002m against a $5,991-6,011m guide and a $6,004m consensus), non-GAAP operating income ($1,502m against $1,497-1,508m and $1,504m), ending ARR ($6,604m against $6,603-6,612m) and net new ARR ($1,352m against $1,350-1,359m). The one departure is free cash flow: the base takes 28.5% against a guide of at least 30%, because reaching 30% for the year requires a 33.0% fourth quarter against 28.8% a year earlier, and the base assumes Q4 repeats last year's margin.

Implied dollar-based net retention is an output of the model, and Section 17.1's ARR path requires 116.8% in FY2027, 110.2% in FY2029, 106.8% in FY2031 and 103.1% in FY2036 in the base case, against a disclosed series of 125% (FY2023), 119%, 112% and 115% (FY2026). The FY2027 requirement is consistent with two quarters of sequential improvement from 115%. The base's decline to 103% by FY2036 puts CrowdStrike below the 110-116% band that Elastic and Zscaler converged into within four to five years of leaving hypergrowth; the bear's decline to 100% means gross expansion exactly offsets churn at a 97% gross retention rate.

Against the reference class of 48 US-listed software companies at $3-8bn of revenue growing 20% or more:

Horizon Bear Base Bull Class distribution Consensus
Revenue CAGR, three years to FY2029 18.1% 21.9% 26.9% p25 14.6%, median 20.8%, p75 24.8% (n=31) 22.8%
Revenue CAGR, five years to FY2031 13.3% 18.7% 24.7% p25 12.1%, median 20.6%, p75 26.0% (n=16) 22.5% to FY2030
Revenue CAGR, seven years to FY2033 10.7% 16.4% 22.3% median 13.9% across software, 17.7% in the subscription subclass (n=12) no coverage

The base is at about the 60th percentile over three years and the 45th over five. Two of fifteen companies in that class held 20% growth for five consecutive years past $3bn of revenue.

Against the company's own incremental-margin record. Realized incremental non-GAAP operating margin (the change in non-GAAP operating income over the change in revenue) was 23.2%, 20.2%, 37.4%, 24.5% and 19.4% in FY2022-FY2026, and 41.3% in H1 FY2027; excluding the $53.4m of realised commission benefit, the H1 figure is about 32%.▪ The base models 38.3% in FY2027 (management's own guide, including the commission change), then 26.3%, 29.9%, 31.1% and 30.3% at FY2028, FY2029, FY2031 and FY2036. No base year exceeds the historical best of 37.4%, and seven consecutive years above the five-year median of 23.2% is an assumption about sustained operating leverage the last three reported years did not deliver. The bull exceeds the historical best in FY2034-FY2036 (39.0-40.2%), which is the assumption most worth distrusting inside it.

Against management's own milestones: the base reaches $10bn of ending ARR in FY2030, a year before the stated FY2031 date, and the bull in FY2029; the $20bn FY2036 goal is met only in the bull.▪

The five most consequential drivers of terminal operating income are all volume drivers, and endpoint growth is worth two-thirds more than the next one: three points a year of endpoint growth is worth $846m of FY2036 non-GAAP operating income, more than 3x the largest cost move inside management's own target bands. The upside and downside are asymmetric because compounding for ten years is convex; the same three points moves FY2036 endpoints to 89.1m or 51.3m against 67.8m in the base. Capex and deferred revenue move only free cash flow. Stock compensation moves only GAAP operating income and, through cash tax, free cash flow the other way: three points less adds $529m to FY2036 GAAP operating income and subtracts $107m from free cash flow, because a higher GAAP profit is a taxed profit.

FY2031 11,358 13,173 (13.8)% 3,093 3,850 (19.7)% 2.445 3.302 (26.0)%

The two match through FY2028 and diverge after, on two drivers. Consensus revenue growth of 24.8%, 22.2%, 21.4%, 21.6% and 21.6% for FY2027-FY2031 contains no deceleration, from a base entering the $8bn-plus band in FY2029 where the class forward three-year median is 17.0%; the base fades to 13.0% by FY2031. And consensus non-GAAP operating margin reaches 27.8% in FY2029 and 30.0% in FY2030 against the base's 26.0% and 26.7%, because the base keeps sales and marketing inside the 28-33% target band instead of driving toward its floor and improves subscription gross margin about 0.2 of a point a year against the one point a year the FY2029 target requires. Consensus keeps FY2029 GAAP EPS at 27% of non-GAAP EPS, five years past the point at which the reference class had cut stock compensation to a median 9.5% of revenue.

18. Risks

Ordered by expected effect on earnings and ARR over the next twelve to twenty-four months, which combines the size of the exposure with the probability that it moves in that window.

1. AI-security demand normalising after the FY2027 pull-forward. Mechanism: the April 2026 frontier-model releases and the coalition CrowdStrike convened afterwards produced what management calls "a deluge of customer, prospect and partner inquiries" and "cybersecurity's Y2K moment" (Q1 FY2027 call). One analyst on the same call described it as "a bit of panic spending, which we're seeing a lot in the consulting industry". Exposure: FY2027 net new ARR guidance moved from $1,239m (+22.5%) to $1,291m to $1,350-1,359m (+34%), a $116m raise in two quarters, and the guide itself implies H2 growth of about 29% after 51% in Q2. A return to the pre-April 2026 22.5% growth rate would produce about $730m of H2 net new ARR against the $766m the guide implies, a $36m difference, 0.5% of ARR. Leading indicators: Q3 FY2027 net new ARR against the $343-347m guide; professional-services revenue growth, which slowed from 23% to 7% in one quarter; the Flex new-logo share of net new ARR; whether AIDR disclosure moves from growth rates to a dollar level. What reduces the exposure: 46% of $10.7bn of remaining performance obligations is due within twelve months, so FY2028 revenue is largely contracted regardless of the bookings path, and multi-year Flex terms plus 97% gross retention hold the base.

2. The DOJ and SEC information requests on revenue recognition and ARR reporting. Mechanism: on the last day of fiscal Q3 FY2024 CrowdStrike booked a $32m order through federal distributor Carahsoft for identity software for the IRS, structured as four $8m payments; the IRS has told investigators it never bought the software (computerworld.com, 2025-02-21, citing Bloomberg, accessed 2026-09-02) [web]. The Q3 FY2025 exclusion of about $26m from ARR, set out in Section 7, involved a distributor in the same federal channel. The 10-Q for the quarter ended April 30, 2025 first disclosed the requests, and the wording is identical in the FY2026 10-K and the Q2 FY2027 10-Q. Exposure: ARR sets management's pay and is management-defined, with contracts in active renewal negotiation staying in the number until the customer gives notice. SentinelOne's June 2023 restatement was 5% of its ARR and cost 35% of its market value in a session. A $26m item is 0.4% of today's ARR; the exposure comes from a control failure or a pattern, not from the size of the first item. Leading indicators: any change in the note's wording, from "requests for information" to a subpoena, a Wells notice or an accrual; a change in the auditor's critical audit matter on subscription revenue recognition; finance-organisation departures; a change in the ARR definition. What reduces the exposure: the securities class action tied to July 19 was dismissed with a final, unappealed judgment in January 2026, and the derivative suits are stayed on the back of it.

3. Microsoft: kernel policy and E5 bundling. Mechanism: two separate channels. Platform policy, where Microsoft's Windows endpoint security platform, in private preview since July 2025 with CrowdStrike among eight partners, is designed to run endpoint protection in user mode; if kernel access is restricted, every third-party vendor re-platforms at once and the architectural difference between Falcon and Defender narrows to what user-mode telemetry allows. And bundling, where Defender ships inside E5 and now the E7 suite, whose two-month launch produced "millions of seats" and a 400,000-seat deployment at EY. Exposure: core Falcon ARR is about $3.66bn, 63% of the total; one point of gross retention on that base is about $37m a year, and on total ARR about $58m. Leading indicators: a Microsoft date for restricting third-party kernel drivers or a general-availability announcement; gross retention returning to a printed number; Gartner endpoint placement; the Microsoft Marketplace ramp, which went from zero in March 2026 to first wins in Q2 FY2027; the E5 refresh cycle. What reduces the exposure: a customer speaking at CrowdStrike's own event tested the switch to Defender and stayed.

4. Frontier-lab disintermediation and agentic pricing. Mechanism: the labs now ship security tooling directly (Anthropic's Claude Code Security announced February 2026, Project Glasswing, OpenAI's Codex Security), and the argument against the incumbents is that automated agents replace the human-delivered layer while identity shifts from humans to agents. Exposure: Falcon Complete and OverWatch plus the $247m professional-services line are the human-delivered revenue most exposed; exposure management competes directly with Mythos-class vulnerability discovery, which had surfaced more than 10,000 high- or critical-severity flaws by late May 2026 (helpnetsecurity.com, 2026-05-26, accessed 2026-09-02) [web]. The cyber ETF declined 5% on the February 2026 announcement. Leading indicators: lab products that include runtime protection and not only code scanning; AIDR pricing changes; the managed-detection gross-margin trend; whether Falcon Complete ARR is ever disclosed. What reduces the exposure: a per-token pricing element already exists inside AIDR, so a shift in the unit of account does not by itself remove the revenue; the margin consequence depends on model-inference costs CrowdStrike does not control.

5. Emerging-line competition after two mega-deals. Mechanism: Google closed Wiz on March 11, 2026 and Palo Alto closed CyberArk on February 11, 2026, so the fastest-growing cloud-security vendor now has hyperscaler distribution and the largest privileged-access vendor is inside a platform that competes across all three emerging lines. Exposure: the trio is 37% of ARR and supplies the growth premium; cloud ARR growth has already declined from above 80% (Q2 FY2025) to above 29% (Q2 FY2027). Leading indicators: cloud ARR growth below 25%; Wiz displacement anecdotes disappearing from the calls; identity growth once Palo Alto's CyberArk cross-sell begins; Sentinel's pricing of first-party data in reply to the AWS default-SIEM placement.

6. Falcon Flex utilisation and what ARR measures. Mechanism: Flex customers commit an upfront pool drawn down across modules, and re-Flex expansions lift ARR before the renewal date. ARR counts the committed run-rate. Exposure: Flex-adopted accounts hold $2.29bn of ARR, 39% of the total, and the first large cohorts renew in FY2027-FY2028. The 10-K states that customers unable to fully use their subscriptions "may elect to renew with shorter subscription periods, fewer cloud modules" and that contraction rises accordingly. Utilisation was last disclosed above 75% at Q2 FY2026, which at $2.29bn would leave up to roughly $0.5-0.6bn of annualised commitment undrawn if the same rate held [estimate: 25% of Flex-account ending ARR; utilisation is measured on contract pools and Flex-account ARR includes pre-Flex subscriptions, so the bases differ and this is an order-of-magnitude maximum]. Leading indicators: net retention printed again as a number; the re-Flex share of net new ARR and the interval to first re-Flex; deferred-revenue additions against ARR growth; any change to the ARR definition.

7. The July 19 aftershock. Mechanism: commitment packages signed in H2 FY2025 with extended terms come up for renewal in FY2027-FY2028, and the 10-K says churn "may occur in future periods". Exposure: about $80m of ARR value granted, $56m of it in Q4 FY2025; incident costs of $60.1m (FY2025), $117.7m (FY2026) and $3.6m in H1 FY2027 net of insurance; a $13.1m accrual at July 2026. Delta's Georgia suit survives on gross negligence and computer trespass after the May 2025 ruling and is in discovery, with Delta claiming more than $500m of losses and CrowdStrike's counsel saying the remainder is contractually capped in the single-digit millions; the court has not ruled on the cap. The passenger class actions were dismissed and affirmed on appeal in May 2026 with rehearing denied in June. Leading indicators: gross retention at Q3-Q4 FY2027; the incident line inside general and administrative; a Delta trial date or a summary-judgment ruling on the cap; insurance-renewal commentary, since the 10-K warns coverage may not renew "on commercially reasonable terms".

8. The GAAP-to-non-GAAP gap. Mechanism: stock compensation was $376.9m in Q2 FY2027, 25.6% of revenue, growing 35% against revenue growth of 26%, and unrecognised expense reached $2,880m. The FY2027 non-GAAP operating income guide includes $85-95m from the commission-amortisation change, about 6% of the guide. Exposure: if the market shifts to GAAP or to free cash flow after stock compensation, FY2027 free cash flow of at least 30% of revenue (about $1.8bn) becomes roughly $0.4-0.5bn after a full-year stock-compensation charge at the H1 run-rate [estimate: twice H1's $674.6m]. GAAP EPS consensus for FY2027 declined 18% over three months while revenue estimates rose. Leading indicators: stock compensation above 26% of revenue; the diluted share count; the FY2028 commission benefit fading; GAAP EPS revisions.

9. Leadership churn and founder dependence. Mechanism: the FY2026 10-K names Kurtz as "critical to our future vision and strategic direction" and adds that the Strategic Plan "could negatively affect our ability to recruit and retain skilled personnel". Exposure: product velocity in AIDR, agentic identity and the agentic SOC, a category that did not exist two years ago; the 10-K describes the incident-response team as small and hard to replace. The global CTO left in August 2026 with no named successor and the shares declined 5.6% on the report [web, unverified]; Kurtz's beneficial ownership is under 1% and he sold $290.6m in eighteen months. Leading indicators: a named CTO successor; Form 4 activity from officers other than Kurtz; departures in engineering or corporate development; retention grants in the FY2027 proxy.

10. Infrastructure commitments and the AWS relationship. Mechanism: about $7.0bn of non-cancelable purchase commitments against $5.0bn of cash, with the FY2028 tranche at $843m, counterparties undisclosed and the composition bundled with advertising, technology, equipment and consulting. The 10-K states that AWS renewal "may be on terms that are significantly less favorable". Exposure: the subscription gross margin. Subscription cost of revenue rose 23% in Q2 FY2027 on hosting (+$13.9m) and data-centre depreciation (+$10.4m), and the FY2029 target of 82-85% non-GAAP subscription gross margin assumes the contracted capacity is used. A growth slowdown against a fixed capacity base compresses the margin by one to two points. Leading indicators: the next purchase-commitment disclosure; capex against the 7-8% guide; the non-GAAP subscription gross-margin trend; any disclosure of the AWS renewal date or terms.

11. Federal and government exposure. Mechanism: the 10-K devotes a full risk factor to government sales (FedRAMP, DoD Impact Level 5, clearances, source-code transparency, administration change) and names "temporary or permanent debarment from sales to government organizations" among possible regulatory outcomes; the regulatory requests in risk 2 are centred on a federal deal through a federal distributor. Exposure: undisclosed. Federal and state revenue is not broken out anywhere; the anchors are 25 of 50 US states standardized on Falcon, an eight-figure new-logo agency win in Q1 FY2027, and "a strong federal quarter" (Q3 FY2026). Leading indicators: October-quarter federal commentary; any regulatory development that touches procurement eligibility.

12. A second platform defect. Mechanism: the FY2025 10-K disclosed a second, smaller defect, a TLS issue in certain Linux sensors fixed by advisory in February 2025, and states that resiliency enhancements "may not be effective". Exposure: the 2024 precedent is net new ARR of $153m in Q3 FY2025 against $223m a year earlier, and $178m of incident cost over two years. Insurance terms after a second event are unknowable. Leading indicator: content-deployment control disclosures and any new sensor advisory.

13. Digital sovereignty and AI regulation. Mechanism: the FY2026 10-K added "digital sovereignty requirements... emerging in the EU" and the FY2025 10-K added regulation targeting "critical infrastructure software resiliency and concentration risk", a post-July-19 policy theme. Exposure: international revenue is 35% of Q2 FY2027 revenue, EMEA 18% and growing 40.0%; the operational response is a sovereign deployment on Schwarz Digits' STACKIT announced March 2026, whose build cost is not separately disclosed. Leading indicator: EMEA growth against the group, and any national procurement rule that requires local processing.

14. Acquisition integration and acquired-ARR opacity. Mechanism: six acquisitions closed between March 2024 and February 2026 for about $1.5bn, plus the pending XM Cyber assets. Acquired net new ARR has been disclosed once, for Q1 FY2027 at $7.8m, so the organic growth rate of Next-Gen Identity and of AIDR cannot be verified from the disclosures. Exposure: FY2027 non-GAAP guidance includes $74-80m of integration expense; goodwill is 18.7% of total assets and is tested against a single reporting unit, so a failed tuck-in would not register. Leading indicator: whether any later quarter separates acquired from organic ARR.

How these move together. The scenario that produces a large drawdown is a single print in which net new ARR lands at the guide instead of above it, while AI-security pipeline commentary softens, cloud ARR growth prints below 25% with a Wiz or Microsoft anecdote attached, the regulatory note changes wording or an accrual appears, and another senior departure is reported. Each of those four has occurred once in the last four quarters. The risks that would resolve together are the regulatory requests closing without action, Delta being capped, and a CTO being named, and none of them adds to ARR.

19. Source disclosure

Primary filings. Seven 10-Ks (FY2020-FY2026), the twelve most recent 10-Qs (fiscal Q3 FY2023 through Q2 FY2027) and the June 2019 S-1 and 424B4 prospectus, which is the only source for FY2017-FY2019. Seven DEF 14A proxies (2020-2026), six 8-K vote reports, and 226 Form 4 filings from February 2025 to August 2026 pulled from EDGAR.

Company communications. All thirty earnings calls from Q1 FY2020 (July 2019) through Q2 FY2027 (August 2026); twenty-nine are from BamSEC and the Q2 FY2023 call of August 2022 is from Quartr, which is noted where it is cited. Forty-seven presentation transcripts from December 2019 to March 2026, covering every investor briefing the company has held through the research cut-off; the Fal.Con 2026 briefing of 2026-09-02 is not in the archive. Twenty-three earnings releases (Q4 FY2021 through Q2 FY2027). Sixteen investor decks with 902 rendered slides, from the October 2020 cloud product briefing to the Q2 FY2027 results deck.

Structured financials and market data. XBRL company-facts extracts for CrowdStrike and the peer set, dated 2026-08-29, used as a cross-check against the filings, which win wherever the two differ. Bloomberg consensus, prices, ratings, bond quotes and analyst recommendations, pulled from a live terminal on 2026-09-02.

Peer and value-chain sources. Filings on disk for Palo Alto Networks, SentinelOne, Zscaler, Fortinet, Okta, CyberArk, Elastic, Cisco, Microsoft, Amazon, Alphabet, Datadog, ServiceNow and Verisk. Peer earnings transcripts exist for Palo Alto (forty) and Datadog (twenty-eight); Microsoft's and the other peers' calls were read through published third-party transcripts where cited.

Data built from those sources. A ten-year annual financial series and a twelve-quarter series reconciled across the filings, the XBRL extracts and the earnings releases; a quarterly guidance-against-delivery scorecard covering twenty-two quarters assembled from the earnings releases; a forty-eight-company software reference class of annual fundamentals from Bloomberg for the base rates; a forty-one-row public comparable table; and the daily price and forward-consensus series behind the four charts in Section 15.

Gaps. No sell-side research on CrowdStrike exists in the local store, so every consensus figure comes from Bloomberg alone and no dated price target or estimate-revision reasoning from an individual house is available. No Daloopa workbook exists for the company, so the three-source reconciliation used the earnings releases as the third source. No 10-K redline dashboard exists, so the year-over-year risk-factor comparison in Section 18 was built directly from the seven filings. Bloomberg publishes no free-cash-flow or operating-cash-flow consensus for CrowdStrike and no line at all for ending ARR, net new ARR, retention, module adoption, Falcon Flex or remaining performance obligations, which is most of what management guides on. No structured guidance extract exists for three quarters (Q4 FY2023, Q1 FY2027, Q2 FY2027), whose guided ranges were read directly from the earnings releases and transcripts. IDC's modern-endpoint share reports for CY2023, CY2024 and CY2025 are paywalled, Gartner's own forecast pages return HTTP 403 so the Gartner spending figures here are secondary relays, and the Leaders lists for the 2025 SIEM, CNAPP and PAM Magic Quadrants could not be retrieved.

Web sources. About thirty distinct domains, all accessed 2026-09-02 and listed with their passages in Appendix B. The heaviest are crowdstrike.com for pricing, press releases, the incident root-cause analysis and the Charlotte AI product page; microsoft.com and blogs.windows.com for endpoint share and the Windows security platform; prnewswire.com and investing.com for Palo Alto's results and call. Pricing evidence comes from aws.amazon.com and docs.aws.amazon.com (marketplace rates and listing fees), siemcostcalculator.com and realm.security (SIEM rate cards), softwarecontractnegotiation.com (cloud-workload tiers), and vendr.com and costbench.com (buyer-side benchmarks). The remainder are valueaddvc.com for Wiz, cisco.com investor relations for Splunk's ARR, fool.com and investing.com for peer transcripts, six news sites, and stockanalysis.com as a consensus cross-check.

Tagged [web, unverified]. One claim: the August 20, 2026 departure of global CTO Elia Zaitsev after thirteen years to launch a $170m AI-cybersecurity venture fund with two former CrowdStrike corporate-development executives, the 5.6% share-price decline on the report, and the absence of a named successor. Both source pages (invezz.com and simplywall.st) return HTTP 403 and the claim could not be re-checked; the June 2026 appointment of Bartley Richardson and Kurtz's description of "our long planned and mutually agreed upon CTO leadership transition" are confirmed in the Q1 and Q2 FY2027 calls.

Estimates by method. Seventy figures above are tagged [estimate: …], each with its method and, where the input is a range, its bounds. By method:

  • Eleven are residuals or differences of management's rounded "more than" product-line minimums: core ARR, the trio's dollar adds, and its share of net new ARR.
  • Twenty-four are unit counts or realized prices triangulated from list rate cards, marketplace pricing and disclosed deal anchors, together with the per-unit gross profits and margins derived from them.
  • Twelve are line-level or segment gross margins and cost shares constrained only by a reported blend.
  • Nine are market sizes, shares or concentration measures built from CrowdStrike's own revenue, its last published share and disclosed peer figures.
  • Six are cost or fee decompositions applied from a disclosed percentage to a reconstructed base: hosting cost of revenue, marketplace fees and reseller capture.
  • Eight are arithmetic on two disclosed figures whose inputs are rounded or dated differently: the return decomposition, the commitment-absorption arithmetic, the Wiz dollar add and the incentive-plan add-back.

Corrections against other sources. FY2025 non-GAAP operating income has two published values, $837.7m as reported in March 2025 and $879.9m as recast in March 2026 after employer payroll taxes on stock awards were moved into the exclusions; FY2025 non-GAAP EPS is $3.93 as reported and $3.24 as recast at a 21% assumed tax rate. FY2024 and FY2025 GAAP results were revised in the FY2026 10-K for a stock-compensation timing error, so FY2024 operating loss widened from $(2.0)m to $(19.1)m and net income declined from $89m to $72.2m; the FY2024 quarterly figures were never revised and no longer sum to the revised annual. The four-for-one split, effective on the ex-date of July 2, 2026, makes per-share history two-basis, and pre-split figures appear in every filing through Q1 FY2027. Bloomberg's estimate snapshot labels CrowdStrike years by the calendar year in which most of the fiscal year falls, so its "CY2026" row is FY2027, and its headline EPS type for CrowdStrike is GAAP, which differs from the non-GAAP figure by a factor of twelve.

20. What we still don't know, and the monitoring KPIs

Ten things about the company that are not in the public record, each with the disclosure that would settle it.

  1. The protected-endpoint count and realized price per endpoint over time. The estimate spans 20-40m because the direct and MSSP price anchors differ by 3-5x and the mix between them is undisclosed. Every unit-economics figure, the market-share arithmetic and the model's largest driver inherit that range. Would close it: a sensor count, or a realized-ASP series, or a resumption of the subscription-customer count on the pre-FY2024 basis.

  2. US federal and state revenue. Not disclosed anywhere, and three separate exposures depend on it: the regulatory requests centred on a federal deal through a federal distributor, the $26m ARR reversal that involved a federal-space distributor, and the 10-K's debarment language. Twenty-five of fifty US states are standardized on Falcon and no dollar figure attaches to that. Would close it: a public-sector revenue disclosure, or federal obligations data by agency and fiscal year.

  3. MSSP unit economics. The channel went from under $100m to more than $1.3bn of business in three years, roughly a quarter of ending ARR, and no price per MSSP-delivered endpoint, no gross margin and no retention figure has been disclosed. An MSSP counts as one customer in both the retention rate and the module-adoption percentages, so the reported KPIs move mechanically with this mix. Would close it: MSSP-delivered ARR with its own retention and margin, or a restatement of the two KPIs excluding MSSP end customers.

  4. Whether the FY2027 acceleration is new demand or re-Flex timing. First re-Flex comes seven to eight months into a contract, well before renewal, at a 25% uplift, and 630 accounts have re-Flexed at least once, 6x the year-earlier count. H1 FY2027 net new ARR was $588.6m against $414.8m. If a material share is expansion that would otherwise have landed in FY2028, the consensus FY2028 step-down is arithmetic and not a demand judgment. Would close it: net new ARR split between new logos, first-time module adds and re-Flex uplift.

  5. AIDR's ARR level. The headline driver of the FY2027 acceleration is supported only by two of the company's own telemetry figures, more than 400% growth in Claude usage and more than 100% growth in custom agent usage on protected endpoints, plus pipeline adjectives. Three sequential growth rates have been published and no dollar level. Would close it: AIDR ending ARR, or the AI-security line broken out in the product-line disclosure.

  6. Organic against acquired ARR. Six acquisitions closed between March 2024 and February 2026 for about $1.5bn, and acquired net new ARR has been disclosed once, at $7.8m for Q1 FY2027. Identity's re-acceleration to 33-34% and AIDR's growth both come from acquired product lines. Would close it: an acquired-ARR line in the quarterly disclosure, or standalone ARR at acquisition for the six deals.

  7. What is inside the $7.0bn of purchase commitments. The note bundles data-centre capacity with advertising, technology, equipment, office renovations, corporate events and consulting, names no counterparty, and gives no take-or-pay terms. The FY2029 subscription gross-margin target of 82-85% assumes the capacity is used, and no disclosure allows that to be tested at a lower growth rate. Would close it: a split of the commitment by category and counterparty, or an AWS contract term and renewal date.

  8. Falcon Complete's scale and economics. The managed-detection franchise produces the labelled corpus behind the data advantage in Sections 2 and 3, and it is one of the seven demand drivers in Section 1; its ARR, endpoint count, price premium and gross margin have never been disclosed. The only quantification is more than 15m labelled annotations a year. Would close it: managed-services ARR, or a services attach rate.

  9. Dollar-based net retention as a number. Given as a figure exactly once since Q2 FY2024, and described as "improved sequentially" in both FY2027 quarters. Retention is the company's direct measure of expansion, and the model's ARR path is checked against it. Would close it: the quarterly figure, printed.

  10. International economics beyond the growth rate. EMEA is 18% of revenue growing 40.0% and is the largest single support for the forward group growth rate, and the sovereignty build-out cost, the European competitive set, the distributor pricing model used outside the US and the currency exposure on non-dollar operating expenses are all held at the group average. Would close it: regional gross margin, or a disclosure of revenue invoiced in non-dollar currencies.

Monitoring KPIs, in the order they would move. Professional-services revenue growth, already at 7%. Net new ARR against the Q3 FY2027 guide of $343-347m. The Flex new-logo share of net new ARR and the re-Flex interval. Core ARR growth against the trio's. Cloud Security ARR growth against 25%. Dollar-based net and gross retention, if printed. Current remaining performance obligations against ARR growth. Non-GAAP subscription gross margin against the 82-85% FY2029 target. Capex against the 7-8% guide. Stock compensation as a share of revenue. And, outside the company, IDC's modern-endpoint share for CY2025, Microsoft's timetable for the Windows endpoint security platform, and whether Fortinet, Zscaler and Cloudflare hold their accelerations, because if the cohort rolls over together the driver was never company-specific.

Two limitations that bear on specific conclusions. The third-party market-share layer in Sections 3 and 4 stands on two figures, Microsoft's own 28.6% for CY2024 and CrowdStrike's own 17.7% for the year to June 2022, and no independent series covers the intervening years, so the share-path comparison cannot be closed. The long-range targets quoted in Sections 6, 14 and 17 were set at Fal.Con briefings between 2023 and 2025 and last restated at Fal.Con 2025 in September 2025; the Fal.Con 2026 investor briefing was held on 2026-09-02 and could re-base product-line ARR, module adoption, the FY2029 margin model or the FY2031 ARR ranges.

Appendix A — Investor-presentation insights and key slides

Sixteen decks with 902 slides run from the October 2020 cloud product briefing to the Q2 FY2027 results deck, and include every investor briefing the company has held except Fal.Con 2022, for which only the transcript is on file, and Fal.Con 2026, which post-dates the research cut-off. Eleven things appear there and nowhere in the filings or the calls.

  • Falcon Flex is priced only in the decks. The 10-K names it once, as a "flexible subscription offering". The decks give the terms (one to five years, swappable modules, a minimum total spend commitment, no annual minimums, the same ARR and revenue recognition as non-Flex), the uplift ladder, and four named case studies with dollar figures, including the conglomerate that moved $5m to $24m to $57m of ARR while contract value moved $14m to $103m to $246m. Contract value and ARR are not proportional and this is the only place both are shown for the same account. See §1.3.
  • The customer commitment packages have an impact matrix. One slide maps each incentive (module adds, professional services, flexible payment terms, term elongation, discounting) to its effect on ARR, revenue, gross margin and cash, and three priced examples show how it worked: a healthcare contract whose term went from twelve to thirteen months for the same $460k of contract value, cutting ARR from $460k to $425k with no revenue reduction. It shows why ARR and revenue separated. See §18.
  • Twenty-four quarters of gross and net retention, FY2018 to FY2023, exist only on two deck slides. Gross retention climbed from 93.9% to 98.3% and stayed in a 97-98% band; net retention peaked at 147.1% in Q4 FY2019 and declined in every multi-year window since, to 115% at January 2026. Expansion, not churn, is what changed. See §3.1.
  • Module adoption on the pre-FY2023 basis. The 4-plus, 5-plus and 6-plus series for FY2018-FY2022 appear only in the decks, so the continuous 6-plus run from 6% (FY2019) to 51% (Q2 FY2027) is half deck and half call. The decks also confirm that every adoption rate excludes Falcon Go customers, defined as organisations with 100 endpoints or fewer. See §1.6.
  • Customer cohort economics by ARR band, with counts, ARR and average module count for FY2017, FY2022 and FY2023, plus the minimum ARR to rank as a top-25, top-100 or top-400 account across five years. No filing discloses the split. See §1.6.
  • The professional-services conversion ratio is quantified. Subscription ARR earned per dollar of initial incident-response or proactive-services spend: $2.97 (FY19), $3.73, $5.51, $5.71, $6.07 (FY23). The 10-K asserts the lead-generator claim without ever sizing it, and the metric was retired after April 2023, so it has never been published for a post-incident cohort. See §1.6.
  • The whitespace ratio has been compressing. Install-base opportunity against ending ARR went 2.5x (FY21), 4.1x, 4.7x, 6.8x (2Q24), then 5.4x (2Q26). The definition also broadened over the last two years, from "endpoint counts" to "endpoint, workload, and identity counts", with no restated prior period, so the like-for-like compression is larger. See §3.1.
  • Logo penetration by segment, the same four-panel slide across four years, shows mid-market penetration moving about one point a year and the small-business panel unmoved below 1% for four years, despite Falcon Go being built for that segment. See §4.5.
  • Named-vendor endpoint shares. One April 2023 slide gives the mid-2022 IDC top ten with vendors named: CrowdStrike 17.7%, other next-generation vendors 7.4% (VMware Carbon Black 4.6%, SentinelOne 2.8%) and legacy signature vendors 46.7%, of which Microsoft is 16.4%. Per-vendor share figures appear nowhere else, and the concentration arithmetic in §4.1 is built on this slide.
  • Charlotte AI's list price of $20 per endpoint per year with a query allocation and paid query packs is one of only two per-module prices the company has published. See §1.1.
  • Forecasts the decks made that can now be marked. The $3bn ARR path (FY2025) was met early; the $5bn path (FY2026) was met at $5.25bn; the required retention rates for that path were cleared. Three were missed: free cash flow margin was forecast at 30% for FY2024 and FY2025 and 30-32% for FY2026 and came in at 26%; stock compensation was modelled to fall to the mid-teens as a share of revenue by FY2026 and was 22.8%; and a September 2023 commitment to "sustained GAAP profit before tax as of FY24" broke with a $(64.2)m pre-tax loss in Q2 FY2026. All three forecasts date from before the July 2024 incident. See §10.4 and §13.

Appendix C — External data sources

Six external datasets are available for a company of this type. None has been pulled.

Web technology and CDN adoption share (W3Techs, BuiltWith, HTTP Archive; free; monthly). Measures the share of public websites running a named vendor's web-infrastructure product over time. For CrowdStrike it measures nothing directly, because Falcon is an endpoint agent inside private corporate estates and does not appear in a public-web technology scan. The nearest use is as a control on the peer set for vendors whose products serve public websites. Partial mosaic.

Developer-ecosystem adoption (npm and PyPI download trends, GitHub activity, developer surveys; free; weekly). Measures the momentum of a vendor's software development kits, command-line tools and platform among developers. For CrowdStrike the relevant surface is the Falcon Foundry application platform, the open APIs and the MCP services described in §2, plus the AgentWorks agent-building layer: download and repository activity would be the first outside evidence on whether the developer platform is being used, against which the only current evidence is a list of named partners. It would inform §2, and §1 where the platform's extension into new modules is the growth mechanism. Partial mosaic.

Search-interest trends (Google Trends; free; weekly). Measures relative search interest for the company and its product names over time and against named peers, on a 0-100 index with no units. For CrowdStrike the useful cuts are Falcon Flex, Next-Gen SIEM and AIDR against Wiz, Sentinel, XSIAM and Defender, as a mindshare proxy on the displacement claims in §4, which depend on CrowdStrike's own call anecdotes. It is directional and not a unit or revenue series. It would inform §4 and §6. Partial mosaic.

Hiring and headcount signals (job postings, LinkedIn, layoff trackers; free; monthly). Measures open roles by function, the total posting trend and headcount actions. This is the closest available outside measure of two things the disclosures leave open: where quota capacity is being added, which bears on the sales-efficiency series in §8 that has halved since FY2022, and where engineering capacity is going by product line, which bears on the roadmap exposure in §2 and on whether AIDR and the agent layer are being staffed at the scale the FY2031-FY2036 targets imply. Headcount went from 10,698 to 11,706 in six months, and the split is not disclosed. It would inform §1, §10 and §18. Partial mosaic.

Service reliability and outage incidents (status pages, Downdetector, post-mortems; free; event-driven). Measures the frequency, duration and root cause of a vendor's own outages. For a security vendor whose largest single event was a self-inflicted outage, an independent incident count separating self-inflicted from third-party causes is the direct external test of the resiliency claim the FY2026 10-K makes and of risk 12 in §18. It would inform §18 and §3. Partial mosaic.

Internet traffic and usage telemetry (Cloudflare Radar, Similarweb, app-store estimates; free; monthly). Measures third-party or vendor-published telemetry on internet and application traffic, including bot and AI-crawler share. For CrowdStrike the relevant series is AI-agent and crawler traffic growth, which is the external counterpart to the company's own claim that agents create greenfield sensor demand: §1.6 flags that driver as a hypothesis and §20 names AIDR's undisclosed ARR as the gap. A third-party agent-traffic series would not size AIDR, and it would establish whether the underlying volume is growing at the rate management's own endpoint telemetry reports. It would inform §6 and §1. Partial mosaic.
